0.title: That You May Know: The Epistle of Assurance
0.overview:
There is a letter in the New Testament that reads like the heartbeat of an old man who has seen everything and lost nothing. John, the apostle whom Jesus loved, the one who leaned against the Lord at the Last Supper, the one who stood at the foot of the cross when the others had fled (John 13:23; 19:26), writes at the end of a long life with the urgency of a man who knows that what he carries is the most important thing in the world. He has handled the Word of Life with his own hands. He has seen the glory. And he cannot be silent.

The First Epistle of John was written to a community under assault, not from Rome, but from within. Teachers had arisen who denied the full humanity of Christ, claiming that the eternal Son had not truly come in the flesh, that the spiritual and the material could not really meet. They were sophisticated, confident, and wrong. After they left, John wrote to those who remained, not to condemn those who had gone but to assure the faithful: you are not the ones who have missed the truth. The letter is saturated with the word “know”, used over thirty times. John wants his readers to know that they have eternal life, that they are in fellowship with the Father and the Son, that the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

But assurance in John is never cheap. It is tested by three great evidences that run through the letter like interwoven cords: the moral test (do you walk in the light, keeping his commandments?), the social test (do you love your brothers and sisters?), and the doctrinal test (do you confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh?). These are not conditions for salvation but symptoms of it: the fingerprints of new birth on a redeemed life. The person who has truly been born of God will love, will obey, and will confess. Not perfectly (John is the one who tells us that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves), but genuinely and persistently.

At the theological centre of the letter stands the cross. “The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1:7). “He is the propitiation for our sins” (2:2). “He laid down his life for us” (3:16). “He loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (4:10). John circles back to the atoning death of Christ again and again, because the cross is the ground of everything: fellowship, forgiveness, assurance, love. The love of God is not an abstraction in 1 John; it is a specific act: the sending of the Son into the world to bear the wrath that our sins deserved so that we might live through him.

1 John was written to produce settled, humble, joyful assurance in the hearts of those who have truly come to Christ, and such assurance, far from producing complacency, is the very fire that fuels a life of love.

1.title: The Word of Life and the God of Light
1.text: <sup>1</sup>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—<sup>2</sup>the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—<sup>3</sup>that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.<sup>4</sup>And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.<sup>5</sup>This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.<sup>6</sup>If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.<sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.<sup>8</sup>If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.<sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.<sup>10</sup>If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1.overview:
The letter opens with a declaration, not a greeting. John insists four times on the physical reality of what he witnessed: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. The eternal Word became someone John could hold. Against teachers who claimed a higher spiritual knowledge and despised the body, John’s answer is the incarnation.

The purpose is fellowship with the Father, the Son and one another. Then comes the first test: God is light, with no darkness at all. Any claim to know him that is comfortable with sin is self-deception. But the answer to sin is not despair. The blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin, and God forgives all who confess.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any command or warning, John rests the whole letter on one fact: the eternal Word became audible, visible and touchable. John writes as a man who was there, so that his readers would share the fellowship he has with the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Incarnation as the Ground of Fellowship

The eternal life was heard, seen and touched. A Christ who did not truly come in the flesh could not truly die for our sins, and without that death there is no fellowship with God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Teachers were spiritualising Christ out of his humanity.

Now: The gospel is not a philosophy but a report of what was heard and seen.

verseByVerse.quote: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 John 1 lays the foundation: the reality of Christ and of fellowship with God. The eternal Word of life became visible, and the apostles heard, saw and touched him (vv. 1–2). They proclaim him so that readers may share their fellowship with the Father and the Son, and their joy be complete (vv. 3–4). God is light (v. 5), and that exposes three false claims (vv. 6, 8, 10), each met by grace: Jesus’ blood cleanses (v. 7), and God is faithful and just to forgive the one who confesses (v. 9). The chapter that begins with God’s Son touched by human hands ends with sinners touched by his blood.

The setting. The writer is John, son of Zebedee, the beloved disciple, writing as an old man (he calls his readers little children, 2:1) to churches in Asia. A group had left the church (2:19) teaching a false Christ. Some held an early form of docetism (from the Greek dokein, to seem): the belief that matter is evil and that the divine Christ only seemed to have a body. Others followed Cerinthus, a teacher in Asia whom early Christian writers remember as John’s opponent, who taught (according to Irenaeus) that the divine Christ came on the man Jesus at his baptism and left before his death. They claimed special knowledge of God while living carelessly and without love. Irenaeus, passing on a story from Polycarp, tells how John ran out of the baths at Ephesus on seeing Cerinthus inside, saying the building might fall because the enemy of the truth was in it. John writes to assure true believers (5:13) and to give them tests of genuine faith: truth about Christ, obedience, and love.

A sentence that cannot wait for its verb. The Greek sentence that opens the letter is one long, breathless accumulation before the main verb arrives. You do not reach “we proclaim” until verse 3. John piles up the evidence first, like a witness who has waited decades to be asked. No greeting, no name, no thanksgiving: the thing he has to say is too large for pleasantries.

That which was from the beginning. “From the beginning” echoes John 1:1, “In the beginning was the Word”, and behind that Genesis 1:1. John is speaking of the eternal Son, who existed before creation. The letter begins in eternity and moves straight to fingertips. John writes “that which”, not “he who”, because he has in view the whole message about Christ: who he is and what he did.

Which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands. Three senses, rising in intensity, as though John were walking closer. Hearing can be done from the edge of a crowd; seeing needs line of sight. “Looked upon” is a long, careful gaze, the word used in “we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). And “touched” is a strongly physical word, used of groping in the dark. It is the word the risen Lord used when he said, “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see” (Luke 24:39). John is answering those who denied that Jesus had a real body. He and the other apostles touched him, before and after the resurrection (John 20:27). The eternal Son became truly, physically human.

The head on his chest. This is the disciple who reclined next to Jesus at the last supper and leaned back against his chest to ask a question (John 13:23–25). He had felt the Lord breathe. Faced with teachers who said Christ only seemed to have a body, he does not argue from philosophy. He says, in effect: I put my head on him. A man does not lean his weight on an appearance.

Concerning the word of life. “Word of life” is Christ himself, the Word (John 1:1, 14), who is life and gives life (John 1:4; 11:25; 14:6). It is also the message about him, and John will not let the two be separated. The message is not a set of ideas a man once taught; the message is the man.

The life was made manifest, and we have seen it. “Made manifest” means made visible: the incarnation. Eternal life was invisible, as God himself is invisible; in Jesus it walked into Galilee. The eternal life of God did not stay where it was safe. Not a teaching about life but the life itself appeared, with a face and a voice and calloused hands.

And testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life. “Testify” is the courtroom word from which martyr comes; “proclaim” is to bring news. The apostles are witnesses in a court and heralds in a street. Early tradition says John alone of the twelve died old, and his brother James was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2). Men do not die for what they know they invented (see the question below).

Which was with the Father and was made manifest to us. “With the Father” means face to face with the Father, the same phrase as John 1:1, “the Word was with God”. The Son is distinct from the Father, yet eternal and divine. The life that appeared to fishermen had come from the Father’s side, where it had been for ever.

How can I know the apostles were not mistaken or lying? Look at what their testimony cost them and what it claimed. They were not describing private visions that no one could check; they spoke of things done in public, within living memory, among hostile witnesses; and as far as our sources tell us, no one ever produced the body, though that would have ended the matter. Paul, writing barely twenty-five years after the events, could point to more than five hundred people who had seen the risen Lord, most of them still alive to be asked (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), so this was not a story the church invented generations later. They gained nothing from it in this world but beatings, prison and death, which rules out deliberate fraud, though suffering alone cannot rule out sincere error. Their accounts have the untidiness of real testimony: the disciples look slow and frightened, women are the first witnesses, which an inventor in that culture would hardly have chosen. None of this compels belief, and it is fairer to say so: it is strong evidence, not a proof, and it is the kind of evidence people rightly trust in a court. And the Spirit who inspired them still bears witness through their words to those who read them (John 15:26–27; 1 John 5:6). Faith is not a leap in the dark. It is trust in reliable witnesses about a real man.

I never saw or touched him. Is my faith second-hand? It is not second-class. John writes these very words so that people who never saw can share exactly what he had (v. 3), and the Lord himself pronounced a blessing over you in the room where Thomas touched him: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29). You know him through the same Word and the same Spirit. The apostles’ eyes were the window God built once, so that everyone afterwards could see through it.

For worship. The hands that flung the stars into place were held out to be touched. He let fishermen jostle him in a boat and Thomas put a finger in the wound. The eternal life of God came near enough to be handled, near enough to be nailed, and it is in that flesh, risen and glorified, that he sits now at the Father’s right hand. The Word of life has a human face, and he has not put it away.
verseByVerse.note: The letter does not name its author, but its language is so close to John’s Gospel that it has long been received as the apostle John’s, written late in the first century, probably from Ephesus. Some had left the church denying that Jesus the Christ truly came in the flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you. The main verb of the long sentence (vv. 1–3) arrives at last: we proclaim. He repeats seen and heard: this is not rumour. And “also to you”: what began in a small circle on a lake shore is not to stay there.

So that you too may have fellowship with us. “Fellowship” (koinōnia) means sharing, partnership, communion, having something in common. Luke uses a related word for James and John as Simon’s partners in the fishing (Luke 5:10), sharing the boat and the catch. John proclaims Christ not merely to inform his readers but to bring them in. Christian fellowship is not merely a pleasant hour after the service; it is sharing a common life in Christ, being co-owners in the same inheritance.

And indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. The Father and the Son are named together as equal partners in this fellowship, which no mere man could be. And fellowship with God and fellowship with other believers go together; you cannot have one without the other (v. 7). The way into it is the apostles’ message about Christ; those who reject that message, as the false teachers did, have no fellowship with God (2:22–23).

A circle that was turning before the world began. Before there was a world, the Father loved the Son and the Son delighted in the Father, in the Spirit (John 17:24). To enter the gospel is to be drawn into a circle of love that has been running from eternity. Jesus prayed for exactly this in the upper room, on his way to the cross: “that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us” (John 17:21). Fellowship is God opening his own life and bringing us in, setting places at his own table for rebels. The Son came out from the Father’s side to fetch them, and went to the cross to make them clean enough to sit down. Now men and women who were strangers to God call him Father, and call the eternal Son their brother.

What does fellowship with God actually look like on an ordinary day? It is quieter than people expect. It is speaking to him in prayer and hearing him speak in Scripture, as friends talk. It is bringing him the day’s worries rather than carrying them alone (1 Peter 5:7). It is confessing sin quickly rather than hiding it (v. 9). It is sharing his interests: loving what he loves, grieving what grieves him. And it is enjoyed with his people, at his table, in his house. Fellowship with God does not depend on a feeling of closeness; it is a shared life. The feelings come and go; the sharing does not stop.

Can I have fellowship with God without a church? Not in the way John means. The sentence runs: “fellowship with us”, and “our fellowship is with the Father”. The road into the Father’s company goes through the apostles’ message, and that message gathers people. A Christian alone is like a coal taken out of the fire: it does not stop being coal, but it goes cold. Some cannot attend for illness or persecution, and God meets them where they are. But choosing to stay away cuts you off from the very means God uses to keep you warm (Hebrews 10:24–25).

verseByVerse.quote: And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we are writing these things. The letter is itself part of the proclamation. Every time you open this letter, the eyewitness is still speaking.

So that our joy may be complete. The stated purpose of the letter is joy. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “your joy”; “our” is better supported, and it includes both writer and readers. The apostle’s joy is bound up with the reader’s flourishing. “Complete” means filled to the brim. John writes because he cannot be fully glad until those he loves are fully in the fellowship of verses 1–3. A father is not at peace while one of his children is missing from the table.

The joy of the upper room. Jesus spoke of the same full joy, in the same Greek, on his last night: “These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full” (John 15:11; see also 16:24; 17:13). John was in the room, and decades later is still passing on what he heard. This joy does not depend on favourable circumstances. It comes from sharing the Son’s own life, and no one can take it away (John 16:22). God is not a reluctant giver of gladness: he is the happy God, and he means to make us happy in him for ever.

What if I do not feel joyful? Then you are not unusual, and you are not disqualified. Christian joy is deeper than mood. It can sit alongside grief, as Paul was sorrowful yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10), and it can be buried for a season under illness, depression or loss. Joy is not something to manufacture by trying to feel happy. It grows from its sources: being near God in his word, being honest with him about sin, being with his people. Keep going back to the spring, even when the cup feels empty. The Lord who wants your joy full knows how to fill it, and he knows how to wait.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — God Is Light: Walking in the Truth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first thing John says about God is not a comfort but a blinding claim: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” Then he exposes three things people say to live comfortably without facing that light: that they have fellowship with God while walking in darkness, that they have no sin, and that they have not sinned. But the light that exposes also heals. The blood of Jesus cleanses, and God forgives those who confess.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Light

Three claims keep people from the light: fellowship while walking in darkness, having no sin, never having sinned. The remedy is confession to a God who is faithful and just to forgive.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers claimed an enlightenment that placed them above sin.

Now: Honest confession, not self-defence, keeps a believer in fellowship with God.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you. “From him” is from Jesus: John heard it from Christ, who called himself the light of the world (John 8:12) and whose life made the claim visible. Everything John teaches about sin, love and fellowship rests on this: what God is like, the God we want fellowship with.

That God is light. In Scripture, light represents God’s holiness, purity, truth and glory (Psalm 27:1; 36:9; Isaiah 60:19–20; 1 Timothy 6:16). God is not merely a source of light; he is light in his very nature. The first words he spoke into the dark of creation were “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3), and the closing pages of the Bible show a city that needs no sun, “for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). Between those two pages he shone in a pillar of fire over Israel and on the face of Moses, and then, fully, in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

What light does. Light shows what is there: the dust, the stain you did not know about. It warms. It makes growth possible. And it is pure: you can shine a light into a sewer and the light does not become dirty. All of that is God. He sees everything exactly as it is. He gives life. And he enters our filth without being stained by it, which is why the Son could touch a leper without becoming unclean, and the leper was made clean instead (Mark 1:41–42).

And in him is no darkness at all. A strong double negative: none, not any. Darkness represents sin, falsehood, evil and ignorance. God is absolutely holy: no shadow of sin, no mixture of good and evil, no hidden corners, no moods in which he is less than himself (James 1:17). Every human being has a dark room somewhere; God has none. That is what holy means: set apart, utterly separate from all evil. His eyes are too pure to look on evil with approval (Habakkuk 1:13), and he cannot be talked into thinking sin is small. You will never discover something about him that makes you trust him less. This was aimed at false teachers who treated sin as compatible with knowing God.

If God is light, why does my life sometimes feel so dark? Because the darkness John means is sin, not hard circumstances. A believer can walk through a very dark valley of grief, illness or confusion and still be walking in the light, in John’s sense, because he is walking honestly with God. Scripture expects such seasons and speaks to them: “Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God” (Isaiah 50:10). When you cannot see his face, you can still lean on his name. The darkness around you is not a darkness in him, and it will not have the last word.

Does this make God frightening rather than loving? It makes him trustworthy. A love with dark corners would be a love you could never be sure of; you would always wonder what was hidden. Because God is light, his love is exactly what it appears to be, with no hidden terms. And John will say just as plainly that God is love (4:8). The two are not rivals. At the cross the light did not dim and the love did not hold back: sin was exposed and judged, and sinners were embraced, in the same act.

In everyday life. Pick one thing you would not want God to see: a resentment, a rehearsed conversation. He has already seen it, and has not turned away from you. Say so to him today; verse 7 tells you what waits for you in the light.

For worship. There is no shadow in God, nothing to hide or regret. The burning purity no one can approach (1 Timothy 6:16) is the same light that came down into a stable and walked our roads, and in that light we see what God is: holy and never compromised, yet stooping to the darkest places to bring his people out. He did not shine on us from a safe distance. He entered our night, and at noon on the day he died darkness covered the land while he bore the judgment our sins deserved (Mark 15:33), so that people of the dark might stand in his light and not be consumed.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have fellowship with him. The first of three false claims, each beginning “If we say” (vv. 6, 8, 10). John is perhaps quoting the false teachers’ slogans. But he says we, not they: the habit of saying the right words over a wrong life is not a sect’s peculiarity but a temptation in every human heart, including an apostle’s.

While we walk in darkness. “Walk” means to live habitually: not an occasional stumble but a settled way of life in sin and falsehood, like a man who keeps to the unlit side of the street because he does not want to be seen. Jesus named the motive exactly: “the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil” (John 3:19). The Son of God walked into a world that loved the darkness, and the darkness put him out, for three days. But it could not hold him: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (John 1:5).

We lie and do not practice the truth. To claim intimacy with the God who is light while the pattern of life runs toward darkness is not a theological error; it is a lie. And “practice the truth” (literally, do the truth) is one of John’s most striking phrases: truth in John is not merely believed but done, lived out, embodied (John 3:21).

The lie we tell with our lives. Most people who live this verse have never said anything false aloud. They sing the hymns, pray the prayers, and believe every word of the creed. The lie is not in their mouths but in the distance between their mouths and their days: the husband who leads family devotions and is cruel when the door is shut; the businesswoman who tithes on money she obtained by deceit. John calls it a lie because God hears not only what we say but what our lives say, and the two do not match.

Whoever follows me. John learnt the language of this verse from Jesus, who stood in the temple and said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). Walking in the light is not first a moral standard; it is walking behind a person, and no one can follow someone while walking the other way. The remedy is not trying harder in the dark but turning round to follow him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean any sin in a believer proves he is not a Christian. Verses 8–10 show that believers do sin. It means a settled pattern of living in darkness contradicts a claim to know God.

How do I tell the difference between stumbling and walking in darkness? Ask what you do with your sin. A believer stumbles, sometimes badly and often, but he hates the sin, confesses it, and turns back toward God; it troubles him, and he does not want to be left in it. The person walking in darkness has made peace with it: he hides it, excuses it, renames it, and has no intention of changing. Another test is whether you want God to see. A stumbling Christian, ashamed, still runs toward the light. A man in darkness avoids it. If your sin grieves you and drives you to Christ, that grief is itself a sign of light.

In everyday life. Is there an area of your life you keep in the dark? Name it to God plainly this week, where his Son’s blood waits to wash it (v. 7), and if it grows in secret, tell one trusted believer. Darkness loses most of its power the moment it is spoken.

verseByVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light. The counterpart to verse 6, with two gifts: fellowship with one another, and ongoing cleansing by Christ’s blood. “Walk in the light” is living openly before God, honestly, in truth and obedience, hiding nothing, letting his light expose and correct us. Not sinlessness, but transparency. “As he is in the light”: the light is not a standard we must reach before we may come; it is the place where he lives, and we are invited to live there with him.

We have fellowship with one another. We might expect “with him”. But darkness, that is, pretence and hidden sin, destroys relationships. Two people who are both hiding cannot be close; they can only be polite. When each is honest with God, they can be honest with each other, and the masks come off.

And the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. “Blood” is Christ’s sacrificial death, his life poured out (Hebrews 9:14, 22; 1 Peter 1:18–19). “Jesus his Son”: the human Jesus is the divine Son, against the false teachers who separated them. It was the blood of Jesus, a man who bled like any man, and it was the blood of God’s Son, which is why it can cleanse not some sin but all sin. “Cleanses” is present tense: it keeps on cleansing. Not that we are justified again each time: justification is a verdict God pronounces once, declaring a believer righteous in his sight for Christ’s sake (Romans 5:1), and he never needs to pronounce it again. Rather, the ongoing sins of believers are continually covered by Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10–14), which needs no repeating. “All sin” means every kind.

A spring, not a bucket. The present tense pictures a stream that runs continuously, washing whatever is dropped into it: the provision never runs dry. The hymn speaks of a fountain filled with blood, and the image is right: what Christ did once at Calvary flows on, and it flows on because the work was finished: nothing needs to be added to it.

Why the light is not to be feared. You might expect the light, where everything shows, to terrify a sinner. John says it is the place of cleansing. The darkness is where sin stays and festers; the light is where it is washed. We hide because we think exposure means condemnation. In the presence of the blood of Jesus, exposure means cleansing. We walk in the light, not because we are clean enough to stand in it, but because he keeps us clean while we are there.

Do I have to tell other people my sins to walk in the light? Not everyone, and not everything. Walking in the light is first honesty with God. But it includes being willing to be known by fellow believers rather than keeping up a performance. Confess to those you have wronged, and ask their forgiveness. Have one or two trusted, mature believers to whom you can admit your struggles and who will pray for you (James 5:16). Wisdom is needed: some things would harm others if broadcast, and public confession is for public sins. The aim is not display but freedom from pretence.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have no sin. The second false claim. Not “I have never sinned” (past, v. 10) but “I have no sin”: a denial that sin still lives in us now. The false teachers may have claimed that their special knowledge put them beyond sin, or that what the body does does not affect the spirit.

We deceive ourselves. “Deceive” means lead astray. We fool ourselves, though not others, and it is a terrible blindness, because the man who has deceived himself has no one left to tell him. Everyone else can see it; he alone has stopped seeing it.

And the truth is not in us. To deny our sin is to have no grasp of the truth about God or ourselves. The word of God, which plainly diagnoses every human being as a sinner (Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:23), has not taken up residence in such a person. The gospel begins with acknowledging our sin.

The holiest people feel it most. Not the beginners: Isaiah, the prophet of the holy, cried out that he was lost, a man of unclean lips, when he saw the Lord (Isaiah 6:5). Paul, near the end of his life, called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). The nearer you come to the light, the more of the dust you can see. A Christian who thinks he has little sin left has usually wandered further from the light, not closer.

The one man of whom it is true. There is one person of whom the words “I have no sin” are simply true, and John names him in this same letter: “in him there is no sin” (3:5). Jesus could ask his enemies which of them could convict him of sin (John 8:46), and none could. The claim the false teachers made for themselves belongs to him alone, and he did not keep it as a boast: the sinless one appeared to take sins away (3:5), carrying ours to the cross, and his whole life of perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). So the Christian who says “I have no sin” is not only deceiving himself. He is taking for himself the one title that belongs to the Saviour, and leaving himself no need of him.

Where Christians differ: can a believer become free of all sin before glory? Some Wesleyan and holiness traditions teach that believers can attain entire sanctification, a state in which they no longer sin knowingly. Those who hold it are often deeply earnest about holiness, and their longing to be rid of sin is one every Christian should share; the question is whether Scripture promises it before glory. This commentary’s view: John says plainly that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself. He includes himself, and every believer, in the we. He writes to Christians, and in the same breath he promises forgiveness to those who keep confessing (1:9). When he later says that no one born of God makes a practice of sinning (3:9), he means the settled direction of a life, not sinlessness; the believer still sins, but he no longer lives in it at peace. Believers are freed from sin’s dominion (3:9; Romans 6:14), and they grow in holiness, but sin remains in them until glory (Romans 7:14–25; James 3:2; Philippians 3:12). We should strive for holiness while daily confessing sin and trusting Christ’s blood.

What it does not mean. It does not excuse sin or make it inevitable in every moment. John writes so that we may not sin (2:1). But when we do, we must not deny it.

If I still have sin, am I really a new creation? Yes. The Christian is a new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), with a new heart that loves God, and sin no longer rules him. But sin still lives in him as an unwelcome tenant, and he fights it until he dies (Galatians 5:17). Both are true at once: you are a saint, set apart and loved, and you are a sinner who still needs cleansing. Admitting your sin does not deny your new identity. It is how the new man behaves. Only the new heart hates the old sin enough to confess it.

In everyday life. Ask someone who lives or works with you what fault of yours they notice most. You can bear to hear it, because the blood of verse 7 has already covered it. Do not defend yourself; thank them, and take it to God.

verseByVerse.quote: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we confess our sins. The chapter’s great promise, set against self-deception (v. 8). “Confess” (homologōmen) is literally to say the same thing: to agree, to acknowledge. To confess is to call sin what God calls it, without excuse. The present tense means keep confessing, a habit of life. And it is specific, as the psalmist found: when he kept silent his bones wasted away, and when he acknowledged his sin and did not cover his iniquity, God forgave (Psalm 32:3–5; 51:3–4). Hidden sin does not prosper, but sin confessed and forsaken finds mercy (Proverbs 28:13).

He is faithful. God keeps his promises. He has promised to forgive those who confess (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:12), and he has staked his name on it. Your forgiveness does not depend on how sorry you managed to feel, or on how well you worded it, but on whether God keeps his word.

And just. We might expect “merciful”. But forgiveness is just because Christ has paid for sin (2:2; Romans 3:25–26). When God forgives the one who confesses, he is not setting justice aside: justice has already been done at the cross, and God would be unjust to punish the same sin twice. So the very attribute that once stood against us now stands for us. A sinner who comes in Christ’s name can appeal not only to God’s kindness but to his fairness.

To forgive us our sins. “Forgive” means release, cancel the debt. The sins are not filed for future use. He casts all our sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19); as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (Psalm 103:12).

And to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. “Cleanse” is the word of verse 7. Forgiveness removes guilt; cleansing removes defilement. Both are complete: all unrighteousness, the deeper contamination beneath the surface acts, including the sins we have not yet noticed.

Where Christians differ: must we confess to a priest to be forgiven? Roman Catholic teaching requires confession of serious sins to a priest. Rome holds that the priest does not forgive in his own name but absolves on Christ’s behalf, as his minister, so that the penitent hears Christ’s own pardon spoken to him. This commentary’s view: John directs confession to God: he is faithful and just to forgive. Christ is our only mediator and advocate (2:1; 1 Timothy 2:5). Confessing sins to one another is good and healing (James 5:16), but forgiveness comes directly from God through Christ, not through priestly absolution.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers lose their justification when they sin and regain it when they confess (Romans 8:1). Confession restores the enjoyment of fellowship with God, like a child confessing to a father, not a criminal before a judge.

Must every sin be specifically confessed before it is forgiven? No. The believer’s standing before God was settled once for all when he believed: the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (v. 7), and there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Confession is the way a child of God keeps short accounts with his Father, restoring fellowship, not a ledger in which any sin forgotten remains unpaid. Confess specifically the sins you know, and trust him with the ones you do not; David prayed, “Declare me innocent from hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12).

And what of sins unconfessed at death? A believer is not lost because he dies with a sin he did not name. This verse describes the pattern of a Christian’s life, walking in the light and confessing as God shows us our sin, not an exam we must pass at the end. Our advocate is Jesus Christ the righteous (2:1), and his propitiation covers all our sins. John will open that word in the next verses (2:2); here it is enough to know that Christ has already borne in full what his people’s sins deserved.

What if I keep confessing the same sin? Keep confessing it, and keep fighting it. God’s promise has no limit on the number of times; Jesus told Peter to forgive seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22), and he is not less patient than he asks us to be. But confession is agreeing with God, and God hates the sin, so true confession includes turning from it: removing what feeds it, asking for help, taking practical steps. Repeated failure is not proof that you are not a Christian. A besetting sin can be loved and hated at the same time, and the hating, and the fighting, are the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:19–25; Galatians 5:17). Giving up the fight would be the danger. Each return to him is a sign that grace has not let you go.

I have confessed, but I do not feel forgiven. Then believe the promise rather than the feeling. John does not say that if we confess we will feel forgiven; he says God is faithful and just to forgive. Your feelings may lag behind for weeks, especially after a serious sin, and the accuser will happily remind you of it. Answer him with the cross: the debt was paid there, and God does not collect twice. If something can still be put right with the person you wronged, put it right. Then thank God for his forgiveness, even before you feel it. The feeling usually follows the faith, not the other way round.

Does this not make sin cheap: do wrong, say sorry, carry on? Only if you misunderstand what confession is. To confess is to agree with God about your sin, and God does not think it small; he thought it so serious that the only just way to forgive it was the death of his Son. No one who has understood that price treats forgiveness as a revolving door. The religious person makes the opposite mistake, thinking he must earn the pardon by feeling bad enough or doing better first. The cross answers both: sin is too costly to be cheap, and grace is too free to be bought. Real forgiveness does not make a person careless. It makes him grateful, and gratitude hates the sin that cost so much (Psalm 130:4; Romans 6:1–2).

In everyday life. Before you sleep tonight, name to God specifically where you sinned today, without arguing for yourself. Then read this verse aloud and believe it: he has forgiven and cleansed you. And if your sin wronged someone, put it right with them tomorrow.

For worship. Here is a God whose justice and mercy kiss each other. He does not forgive by looking away from sin but by having looked straight at it on the cross, where he poured out on his Son what we deserved. Every honest sinner who comes finds the door already open and the Father already running. He is faithful, because he cannot lie; he is just, because Christ has paid; and he is glad to forgive.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have not sinned. The third and most extreme claim. Verse 8 denied that sin still lives in us; this denies ever having committed a sin, whether in the whole of life or since conversion.

We make him a liar. God has declared that all have sinned (Romans 3:23; Psalm 14:3; Isaiah 53:6). To deny our sin is to call God a liar and make the cross unnecessary. Pride always, in the end, accuses God.

And his word is not in us. Someone who claims never to have sinned has never really heard God’s word. The good news has not yet reached him because the bad news has not yet landed.

Two men in the temple. One stood and thanked God that he was not like other men, and listed his virtues. The other stood far off, would not lift up his eyes, beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). The first made God a liar without realising it; the second agreed with God and went home justified. Every one of us goes into the temple as one of those two men.

How do I take sin seriously without being crushed by it? Look at your sin only long enough to confess it, and look at Christ for much longer. John never mentions sin in this chapter without mentioning the remedy in the same breath: the blood that cleanses (v. 7), the God who forgives (v. 9), and, as the letter runs straight on, the Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (2:1). A Christian who only examines himself will despair; one who never does will become proud. The healthy pattern is honest about sin and glad about grace, with the gladness the larger of the two. For every look at yourself, take ten looks at Christ.

For worship. God’s word about us is severe, and it is true, and it is the beginning of every mercy. He tells us we have sinned because he has come to forgive sinners, and he will not let us hide from the diagnosis because he is holding out the cure. The Physician came for the man who will say, in agreement with God, I have sinned; and to that man he gives his own righteousness, his Father’s welcome, and a word that lives in him for ever.

1.theology:
The Incarnation as Foundation. Everything in 1 John rests on the physical, historical, tangible reality of the incarnation. John's four verbs in verses 1–2 (heard, seen, looked upon, touched) answer docetism, the early teaching that Christ only seemed to be human. If Christ did not truly come in flesh, the blood shed on Calvary has no atoning value and there is no real fellowship between God and humanity. God became graspable so that we could grasp him, and through him, life.

The God Who is Light. John's declaration that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" shapes how we live. Fellowship with a God of absolute moral purity cannot coexist with a comfortable relationship with sin. The light is searching, and also liberating: in the light, where our sin is exposed, the blood of Jesus cleanses. God's holiness is the backdrop against which his grace shines. You cannot appreciate the gospel without first standing in the light of who God is.
1.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had just experienced a painful split. People they had broken bread with had walked out, leaving wounds and questions: had those who stayed missed the deeper truth? John's answer in chapter 1 is the apostolic testimony: we were there. We heard him, saw him, touched him. The assurance of the community rests not on their spiritual experiences but on the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses of the Word of Life.

Now: We live in a culture that treats feelings and spiritual experiences as the surest guide to what is real. John’s answer is the incarnation: Christianity is tied to history, to flesh, to an empty tomb, and our fellowship with God is a fact, not a feeling. Confession, agreeing with God about what we are, is the daily discipline that keeps it real: not earning forgiveness, but receiving what has already been purchased.

2.title: Our Advocate, Our Obedience, Our Love
2.text: <sup>1</sup>My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.<sup>2</sup>He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.<sup>3</sup>And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.<sup>4</sup>Whoever says “I know him” but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him,<sup>5</sup>but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:<sup>6</sup>whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.<sup>8</sup>At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.<sup>9</sup>Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.<sup>10</sup>Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.<sup>11</sup>But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.<sup>12</sup>I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.<sup>13</sup>I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.<sup>14</sup>I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.<sup>15</sup>Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.<sup>16</sup>For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.<sup>17</sup>And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.<sup>18</sup>Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.<sup>19</sup>They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.<sup>20</sup>But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.<sup>21</sup>I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.<sup>22</sup>Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.<sup>23</sup>No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.<sup>24</sup>Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.<sup>25</sup>And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.<sup>26</sup>I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.<sup>27</sup>But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.<sup>28</sup>And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.<sup>29</sup>If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
2.overview: Chapter 2 moves in three steps. John wants his readers not to sin, but knows they will, and points them to their advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins. Then he gives the marks of real faith: a life that keeps God’s commands, walks as Jesus walked, and loves the brothers. Last, he warns against loving the world, which is passing away, and against the antichrists who have left the church, and urges his readers to abide in what they heard from the beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Advocate and the Test of Knowing God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John writes so that his people will not sin, but he knows they will, so the provision comes with the command: an advocate with the Father, who pleads not our innocence but his own righteousness, and who is himself the propitiation for our sins. On that ground of grace comes the first test: those who know him keep his commandments and walk as he walked.
verseByVerse.theology:
Advocate and Propitiation

Jesus Christ the righteous pleads for us, and he is the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: By separating the divine Christ from the suffering Jesus, the false teachers left the cross with no power to save.

Now: Knowing God shows itself in keeping his commandments and walking as Jesus walked.

verseByVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 John 2 gives tests by which believers may know that they truly know God. If they sin, they have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins (vv. 1–2). Those who know God keep his commands and love their brother (vv. 3–11). John assures them that they are forgiven (vv. 12–14), warns them not to love the world (vv. 15–17), and exposes the antichrists who left the church and deny that Jesus is the Christ (vv. 18–23). The readers have the Spirit’s anointing and must remain in Christ, so as to be confident when he appears (vv. 24–29). The chapter opens with Christ pleading for us in heaven and closes with Christ appearing from heaven, and everything between is how to live in the meantime.

My little children. “Little children” (teknia, dear children) is a tender term, used seven times in the letter, and it sets the pastoral tone at once. Whatever hard things follow, they are said by a grandfather with his hand on a child’s head.

I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. “May not sin” (hina mē hamartēte) points to single acts: may not commit even one sin. Chapter 1 might be misused: if everyone sins and God forgives, why worry? John answers: forgiveness is not a licence. The verse holds two truths together: holiness is the aim, and the provision for failure is already in place. Lose the first and grace becomes an excuse; lose the second and holiness becomes despair.

But if anyone does sin. “If” (ean): John knows believers will sin (1:8, 10). He does not say “when”, because he does not want to sound resigned, and he does not say “never”, because he will not lie. He says “if”, with the remedy already in the next breath.

We have an advocate with the Father. “Advocate” (paraklētos) is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit, the Helper (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7): one called alongside to help, especially a defence lawyer in court. The Spirit is our advocate within us; Christ is our advocate before the Father. When Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), Christ speaks for us. “With the Father” is face to face with him, as in 1:2: our advocate is in the Judge’s presence and is the Judge’s Son. And “we have” is present: he is not sent for in an emergency after we have sinned. He is already standing there for sinners like us.

The scene in Zechariah. The prophet saw it centuries before. Joshua the high priest stood before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, with Satan at his right hand to accuse him. The accusation was true; the clothes were filthy. But the LORD rebuked the accuser: “Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?”, a burning stick snatched out of the flames. And the filthy garments were taken off, and he was clothed in clean ones (Zechariah 3:1–5). That is what happens in heaven when a Christian sins. The charge is not disputed. It is answered.

Jesus Christ the righteous. “The righteous” (dikaion): Christ is perfectly righteous, and that is why he can speak for us. His plea is not that we are innocent, but that he has paid for our sins (v. 2). An ordinary lawyer argues that his client did not do it. This advocate admits everything, and wins, because he pleads not our righteousness but his own: a life of perfect obedience and a death in our place, both counted as ours (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He has never lost a case, and the Father who sent him delights to hear him.

What it does not mean. Christ’s advocacy does not mean the Father is reluctant and must be persuaded. The Father sent the Son in love (4:9–10). His advocacy is his presence there as the one whose sacrifice covers our sins (Hebrews 7:25).

Does having an advocate make sin less serious? It makes it more serious. Look at what it costs: the eternal Son must stand in the Father’s presence with the marks of the nails in his hands, and his plea is his own death. No one who understands that can treat sin lightly. But it changes what sin does to a believer. It no longer threatens his standing, so he is free to stop hiding it. A child who knows his father will not disown him is not more careless; he is more honest. And honesty is where holiness begins.

What does this mean in the moment after I have sinned? It means you go straight to him, not away from him. You do not need to wait until you feel sorry enough, or until you have done a week of better behaviour to earn the right. Your advocate is already speaking for you. Name the sin to the Father, plainly, and thank him that Jesus has answered for it. Jesus told Peter that Satan had demanded to sift him like wheat, and then said, “but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). He prays for you before you fall and while you are down.
verseByVerse.note: “Advocate” is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit (“Helper”) in John’s Gospel; here it is Jesus himself pleading for us.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the propitiation for our sins. The advocate of verse 1 is also the propitiation. He does not merely plead; he has already paid, and the advocacy in heaven rests on an atonement finished on earth. “He is” (autos estin): he himself is the propitiation, not merely its provider. A propitiation (hilasmos) is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. To expiate is to remove the sin; to propitiate is to turn away the wrath. Christ’s death does both, and this word is the stronger one: the holy anger of God against sin has been absorbed, not overlooked. The word is related to the mercy seat in the tabernacle (Hebrews 9:5), the lid of the ark where, once a year, the blood was sprinkled between God’s presence and the broken law. Christ’s death satisfied God’s just wrath by bearing it in our place (Romans 3:25; Hebrews 2:17), which is why the Father can be both just and forgiving (1:9). This is penal substitution: penal, because what Christ bore was the penalty that sin deserves; substitution, because he bore it in the place of others.

Not a pagan bribe. Pagan propitiation meant men trying to calm a moody god with gifts. The biblical propitiation is the reverse at every point. It is not man appeasing God but God providing the sacrifice himself: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (4:10). God’s wrath is not a bad temper but his holiness meeting evil with steady justice, and the one who bears it is the Son who came willingly, and is himself God.

And not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. “Ours” means John and his readers, Jewish and Gentile believers. The words “the whole world” have been argued over for four centuries. But before the argument, see what the verse is for. John is writing to Christians who know they will sin, to keep a failing believer from despair, and on every reading of it the person who trusts Christ is covered.

Where Christians differ: did Christ propitiate the sins of every person? Arminians (Christians who hold that God’s choice of his people rests on his foreknowledge of their faith) and others read the whole world as every individual without exception, so that Christ’s death was a propitiation for the sins of all people, including those who are finally lost. Universalists conclude that all will be saved. Among those who hold to grace, the strength of the wider reading is the plain force of sentences like this one, and of others: he gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6); he tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9); one has died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14). Read without a system, this verse does look as though it is widening something, and honesty requires saying so. Godly, careful men have stood on both sides, and neither side holds its view in order to shrink the cross. This commentary’s view: Propitiation means God’s wrath is actually turned away. If Christ propitiated God’s wrath for every individual, then no one would face God’s wrath, which Scripture denies (John 3:36; Revelation 14:10). So the whole world must mean something other than every individual. In John’s writings, world often means people of every kind and nation, not just Jews. In John 11:51–52 Caiaphas prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad: the same shape of sentence, from the same author, with the same widening. John’s point is that Christ’s sacrifice is not limited to one group, John’s churches, or Jewish believers; it is for people throughout the whole world, of every nation (Revelation 5:9). It is also the only propitiation there is: there is no other sacrifice available anywhere in the world. This is definite atonement: Christ’s death actually and effectively propitiated God for all his people, from every nation. Scripture’s language about the cross points this way throughout: he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21); the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11, 15); Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25); God obtained the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28). Its value is infinite and sufficient for all, and the gospel is offered sincerely to all.

What both sides agree on. It is more than what they disagree on, and it is the part that changes how you live. The death of Christ is of infinite worth: there is no shortage in it, no ceiling, nobody for whom it would have been insufficient. The offer is genuine and it goes to everyone without exception. No one who comes is turned away, ever, for any reason. And nobody at all is saved by any other means.

Then can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for him? Tell him what the apostles told people. They did not open with the extent of the atonement; they proclaimed that Christ died for sinners, that he is a perfect and sufficient Saviour, and that everyone who repents and believes will be forgiven (Acts 2:38; 13:38–39). You can say with complete sincerity: Christ is offered to you; there is room for you; if you come to him he will never cast you out (John 6:37). That is a real offer from a real Saviour, and it is the most generous sentence a human being can hear.

How do I know he died for me? Not by searching the secret decrees of God, but by coming to Christ. Everyone who comes finds that he was expected. The question is not first whether your name is on a list but whether you will take what is held out. If you trust him, rest on him and want him, you have every right to say with Paul that the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). The doctrine was given to comfort believers that their salvation was actually accomplished, not to keep seekers at the door.

For worship. The wrath that should have fallen on us fell, and it fell on him. God did not lower his justice to save us; he satisfied it himself, at his own cost, in his own Son. The cup that was ours he drank to the bottom, and when he cried that it was finished, it was. So the mercy seat is no longer a box hidden in a curtained room but a cross lifted up before the nations, and a multitude from every tribe is being gathered whom he bought. There is a man in heaven who never needs to be reminded of our names; he saves completely, and his blood has never failed for one of those for whom it was shed.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath.

verseByVerse.quote: And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have come to know him. “Have come to know” describes a knowledge gained in the past and still held. The false teachers claimed special knowledge of God; John gives tests by which true knowledge can be recognised. And knowing, in John, is never just having information. It is knowing a person, the knowing of which Jesus said, “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God” (John 17:3). It is astonishing that God can be known at all. The Maker of galaxies is not a theory to be argued about but a person to be met, and he has made himself known in his Son, so that fishermen and housewives and children can say, “I know him.”

If we keep his commandments. “Keep” means observe, guard, obey, and the tense is habitual. “His commandments” are God’s moral will, summed up in love for God and neighbour (3:23; John 13:34; 15:12). This is the first test: obedience. John is not setting up salvation by works; he is describing what a genuine relationship produces (John 14:15, 21). You cannot live for years with someone you love and not begin to care about what he cares about. And knowing him changes us: no one can know this God without beginning to grow like him.

The Son who kept his Father’s commandments. John did not invent this test; he watched it lived. Jesus said, “I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love” (John 15:10), and his whole life, from the carpenter’s bench to the cross, was knowledge of the Father worked out in obedience. The commandments a Christian keeps are a path the Son has already walked. Obedience is the family likeness of the obedient Son.

In the flow. The claim of 1:6, to have fellowship with God, is now tested by obedience (vv. 3–6), by love for the brother (vv. 7–11), and later by belief about Jesus (vv. 22–23). These tests are not hurdles for getting in, but the marks of those who are already in (5:13).

How much obedience is enough to be sure? John does not give a percentage, because he is not grading a performance. He is looking for a direction. The question is not whether you ever fail, since you do, but whether obedience is the settled direction of your desire and effort. Do you want to do what God says? When you see that something is his will, does it matter to you? When you disobey, does it trouble you and send you back to him? A real but weak obedience is evidence of real life. What contradicts the claim to know God is not stumbling but a life that has stopped caring what he commands.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever says I know him. Another false claim, as in 1:6, 8, 10, perhaps the false teachers’ slogan. The words are right; the question is what stands behind them.

Is a liar. Strong language: the claim and the life are irreconcilable, and the truth has not taken hold of him. He has the vocabulary of faith without its substance, like a man who can describe a country in detail from the guidebook and has never set foot in it. John is describing someone who claims God and shrugs at his word, not a believer who fails and grieves over it; that grief is the opposite of what he condemns.

Words first spoken by Jesus. To men who claimed God as their Father while plotting to kill him, Jesus said: “you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you, but I do know him and I keep his word” (John 8:55). All of John’s terms are there: knowing, lying, keeping his word. The true knower of God is Jesus himself, in whom knowing the Father and obeying him never parted by a hair.

Whoever keeps his word. “His word” is broader than commandments: the whole of God’s revealed will. The man in view does not merely obey a list; he treasures everything God has said and lets it rule him.

The love of God is perfected. “Love of God” can mean God’s love for us, our love for God, or the love that comes from God. Probably our love for God, which shows itself in obedience (5:3). “Perfected” means brought to its goal. Love that never reaches the hands has not finished its journey.

That we are in him. This final clause is easily missed. Keeping his commands shows more than good behaviour: it assures us that we are joined to Christ. Obedience tells us we are in him, not just that we agree with him.

What if I obey out of duty, not love? Then keep obeying, and ask God for the love. Duty is not the enemy of love; it is often the scaffolding inside which love is built. A husband who keeps his vows on the days he feels nothing is not a hypocrite but faithful, and the feelings usually return. Jesus himself said, “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15), and the road also runs the other way: those who obey come to know him better, and knowing him they love him more (John 14:21). Tell God honestly that your heart is cold, and do the next right thing.

verseByVerse.quote: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever says he abides in him. “Abides” means remains, dwells, continues, John’s word from the vine and the branches (John 15:4–10): not visiting Christ but drawing life from him all the time.

Ought to walk. “Ought” means owes it, a debt; “walk” is to live; and “he” is emphatic: that man, the one we saw. The test is likeness to Christ (John 13:15; 1 Peter 2:21). It does not come by willpower but grows out of being joined to him: those who abide in the vine begin to bear the vine’s fruit.

The man John watched walk. John is not recommending an abstract virtue. He had walked behind Jesus on the roads of Galilee for some three years. He had watched him stop for a blind beggar the crowd wanted silenced, eat with tax collectors, rise before dawn to pray, weep at a friend’s tomb, wash twelve pairs of dirty feet, and set his face to go to Jerusalem knowing what waited there. When John writes “the same way in which he walked”, he is seeing it. We follow footprints made by the Son of God in the dust of our world.

Is this not an impossible standard? As a way of earning God’s favour, yes, completely. But John is not writing to people trying to get in; he is writing to people who abide in him. The standard is the direction of the life, not the measure of its success. A child learning to write copies the teacher’s letters and makes a mess of them, and the teacher is delighted, because the child is copying the right letters. Christ does not merely set the pattern; he lives in those who follow it, by his Spirit. Where a life runs in a quite different direction from his and stays there, the claim to abide in him should be questioned. Where it is stumbling after him, it is the real thing.

In everyday life. Pick one encounter in the Gospels: the woman at the well, the washing of feet, the leper he touched first. The one who walked that way now lives in you by his Spirit. Look this week for the person in your path whom everyone else is stepping round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — The Old-New Commandment: Love and Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The command to love is old, because it was there from the beginning (Leviticus 19:18), and new, because Christ has given it a new measure (John 13:34) and the true light is already shining. The test of whether we are in the light is concrete: do we love our brother?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Old-New Commandment

The command to love is old, and new in Christ, because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The split in the church showed where the darkness was.

Now: Nursed grudges blind; love keeps the path clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved. This is John’s word of choice when he is about to make a major point, and it is the first time he uses it in the letter. He is about to talk about love, and he begins by calling them loved.

An old commandment. Old means long-established, familiar, theirs “from the beginning” of their hearing the gospel. This is the command to love, rooted in Moses (Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 19:18) and taught by Jesus. Unlike the false teachers with their advanced insight, John keeps returning to the original. God does not change his mind about what is good. His word is old because he is eternal, and it is never stale because he is never tired.

The word that you have heard. The answer to teachers offering something new is not to become cleverer but to sink deeper roots into the apostles’ message already received.

The oldest command in the mouth of Christ. Asked which commandment was the greatest, Jesus did not produce a new one. He reached back to Moses for the two oldest, love the Lord your God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself, and said that all the Law and the Prophets hang on them (Matthew 22:37–40). Then he did what no one before him had done: he kept them, all the way to the cross. So the old command reached John’s readers as part of the news about Christ, and they learnt what love is by hearing about him.

The old man’s one sermon. Jerome tells a story about John in extreme old age at Ephesus. He was too frail to walk to the church meetings, so his disciples carried him in, and he could manage only one sentence: little children, love one another. He said it every time. At last someone asked him, wearily, why he always said the same thing. He answered that it was the Lord’s command, and if this alone were done, it would be enough. Whether every detail is exact or not, the story fits the man who wrote this verse: he had spent a long lifetime discovering that he had not finished obeying it.

Does this mean Christians should not learn anything new? No. We should grow in knowledge all our lives (2 Peter 3:18), and every generation discovers more of what is in Scripture. What John warns against is new content: a gospel beyond the gospel, a secret level of truth that the apostles did not teach. Growth digs deeper into what was given; error builds somewhere else. A good test of any teaching that excites you: does it send you back to the Christ of the apostles with fresh wonder, or does it make the plain gospel seem elementary and leave it behind?

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new commandment. New here means new in quality, not merely recent (John 13:34). It is old in its source, from the beginning, but new in its standard, which is Christ’s love, and in its power, because Christ has brought in the new age and given his Spirit. Moses said love your neighbour as yourself. Jesus said love one another as I have loved you, and then went out and was crucified. The cross is now the measure and the pattern of love.

Which is true in him and in you. “True” here means made real, actually happening. The command is fulfilled in Christ’s life, because he embodied it perfectly, and it is being fulfilled in believers, because the Spirit is now producing it in them. The command was a description waiting for a person; now it has one.

The darkness is passing away. The verb means is going by, disappearing; the present tense pictures it in progress. The old age of sin and darkness is ending.

The true light is already shining. The true light is Christ (John 1:9; 8:12). With his death and resurrection the age to come has already broken in, though this present evil age has not yet ended (Galatians 1:4; Hebrews 6:5). Light and darkness overlap now, but the darkness is fading. So when we love, we are not straining against the way things really are. We are living by the new age that has already arrived in Christ. Hatred belongs to the night that is ending; love belongs to the day that is coming. When you love, you are living in tomorrow.

The grey before dawn. Anyone who has been up before sunrise knows the moment. It is still dark and nothing has visibly changed, yet the sky in the east has thinned, and you know the sun is coming. That is where the church lives: in the grey before dawn, with the first light on the hills.

The world seems to be getting darker. How is the darkness passing? John is reading history by its centre, not the evening news: Christ has risen, and the light cannot be put out. Darkness can still rage as its time runs short (Revelation 12:12), but every person brought out of darkness into his light (1 Peter 2:9) is the dawn spreading, and since the resurrection it has spread to every continent. The darkness is losing, even when it is loud.

In everyday life. Measure your love this week by the new standard, not the old one: not as you love yourself, but as he loved you. Ask what love would cost you today if it looked like his: time, pride, money, the right to be proved right. Then pay it somewhere specific.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever says he is in the light. Another claim, as in verses 4 and 6, now tested by the most uncomfortable measure: the treatment of a fellow believer.

And hates his brother. The tense means keeps on hating: not a passing flash of anger but a settled attitude. Hatred includes contempt, resentment, ill will, refusing to love. His brother is a fellow member of the church, the person on the next chair on Sunday; the false teachers apparently despised ordinary believers. It is easy to love humanity at large. John points at someone with a name.

Is still in darkness. Whatever he claims, he has never left the darkness. This is the second test, love. John does not allow our relationship with God to be separated from our treatment of people.

The brother Christ has made. Hatred of a brother proves a man still in the dark because the light is Christ (v. 8), and the brother is someone that light has claimed: born of God (5:1), cleansed by the blood of Jesus (1:7), and called brother by the Son himself (Hebrews 2:11). To stand in the light is to stand beside Christ and see this person as he sees him. No one can be near the Lord and keep his back turned on the Lord’s family. When we were enemies, God did not wait for us to become likeable. The love that refuses to hate a brother is only the overflow of a love that refused to give up on us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer can never feel anger or have conflict with another believer. It describes a settled attitude of hatred and contempt.

Who is my brother, and may I hate those outside the church? Your brother here is your fellow believer, because John is giving a test of genuine membership in God’s family. But it does not follow that you may hate anyone else. Jesus commands love for enemies and persecutors (Matthew 5:44), and the neighbour of Leviticus 19:18 is whoever is in front of you (Luke 10:29–37). John narrows the focus because love inside the family is the first proof that you belong to it. If you cannot love a Christian who shares your Lord, your claim to love the unbeliever down the road is unlikely to be real.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No cause for stumbling. The word (skandalon) is originally the stick in a trap that springs it. Love keeps us from tripping and from tripping others (Romans 14:13; Psalm 119:165).

Twelve hours in the day. John had heard this picture from Jesus. When the disciples begged him not to go back to Judea, he answered: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world” (John 11:9). He was going to Bethany because Lazarus, whom he loved, had died (John 11:5), and that walk of love led in the end to the cross. Love made his road plain, though not safe, and the loving believer walks the same road behind the same Lord.

How hatred trips us. Think about how resentment actually works in a life. It distorts judgment: you misread the other person’s every move. It makes you avoid church or a family gathering, and so cuts you off from grace. It hands the devil a foothold (Ephesians 4:26–27). Behind many spiritual falls there is a grudge. The loving person is not cleverer; he simply has nothing on the path for his feet to catch on.

What does love for a brother look like when he is difficult? Love is not mainly a warm feeling but a settled will for his good, shown in action (3:18). With a difficult brother that means praying for him honestly, refusing to gossip about him, speaking to him rather than about him, giving him the benefit of the doubt, and forgiving when he wrongs you. It may mean telling him a hard truth gently. It does not mean pretending wrongs did not happen or putting yourself in danger. You can love someone you do not naturally like, because the love comes from God, not from your temperament.

For worship. The one who never stumbled holds the hands of those who do.
