He walked every step of his Father’s will without a slip, and now he goes before his people as the shepherd who knows every stone on the path. He is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24), and he will not loosen his grip on one of us between here and there.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Position and practice. John piles up four statements: he is in the darkness, walks in it, does not know where he is going, and has been blinded.

Does not know where he is going. He thinks he knows; he has strong opinions about everybody. But he is walking in circles.

While you have the light. Jesus spoke these words first, in the last days before the cross: “The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going” (John 12:35). And he gave the remedy with them: “While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light” (John 12:36). A blind man cannot cure his eyes by staring harder into the dark. The cure for hatred’s blindness is faith in the Light himself, while he is near.

Blinded. Hatred blinds, about God, oneself and others (2 Corinthians 4:4). Think of a man who stays in a dark cellar for years: when he finally comes up, the daylight he needs is the very thing he cannot bear, and he turns back to the dark. Hatred does that to the soul. But Jesus spat on the ground, made mud, and gave a blind beggar his sight; he can do the same for a heart blinded by bitterness. No darkness is too long-standing for him, and no grudge too old.

Can I hate someone and not know it? Yes, and that is the frightening part of this verse: blindness does not feel like blindness. Hatred rarely calls itself by name. It calls itself justice, discernment, honesty, or just being realistic about him. Some signs that it is present: you feel pleasure when he fails; you replay his offences; you cannot pray for his blessing; you find yourself telling others about him; you cannot bear to hear him praised. If any of these are true, do not argue with the diagnosis. Ask God to open your eyes, and begin by praying for that person’s good. And take heart: the dismay you feel at finding these signs is itself the light at work, and the Lord who prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34) is able to teach you to forgive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Assurance for Every Stage of Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the tests, John pauses to reassure. He tells little children, fathers and young men what is already theirs: forgiveness, knowledge of the eternal Christ, and victory over the evil one through the word abiding in them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance for Every Stage

Before further commands, John tells every believer what is already his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were being told they needed something more.

Now: The newest believer needs first to hear that his sins are forgiven for Christ’s name’s sake.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am writing to you, little children. After hard tests, John pauses to reassure three groups. Either these are three stages of spiritual maturity, or little children addresses all believers (as in v. 1), and fathers and young men are two groups within the church, older and younger.

Because your sins are forgiven. The Greek word can mean “that” or “because”; probably “because”: John writes to them because they are genuine believers. The tense means have been forgiven and remain forgiven. Forgiveness is the first word to every believer because it is the ground of every other word.

For his name’s sake. “His name” is Christ’s name, his person and work (Acts 4:12; 10:43). Forgiveness is on account of who Christ is and what he has done, not anything in us; God forgives to honour his Son. The God who keeps the stars in their places has staked the honour of his own Son’s name on the pardon of sinners. He does not forgive grudgingly or provisionally, keeping a file in case we disappoint him.

Why the reassurance comes here. John has just put his readers through searching tests, and a sensitive believer begins to tremble. So John stops and says: I am not writing because I doubt you. I am writing because you are forgiven. The tests are not meant to make the children of God unsure, but to show the counterfeit for what it is, and to let the real children see the family likeness in themselves.

What if I am not sure my sins are forgiven? Then look away from yourself to the ground of forgiveness: his name’s sake. If forgiveness rested on the depth of your sorrow or the quality of your faith, you could never be sure. It rests on Christ. Ask yourself: am I trusting him, and him alone, to be my righteousness? If the answer is yes, however weakly, then God’s word says you are forgiven (Acts 10:43), and it is not humility but unbelief to doubt it. Assurance grows by looking at Christ more than at yourself.

In everyday life. When an old sin comes back to accuse you, do not reopen the case. Say aloud: forgiven, for his name’s sake.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers. They are mature believers, perhaps older in years. “Him who is from the beginning” is Christ, the eternal Word of the letter’s opening (1:1). Long years in the faith have not made Christ stale to them; they have rooted them more deeply in him. What John praises in his fathers is not their achievements or their offices but that they know him.

Young men. They are believers in the vigour of spiritual life, perhaps younger in years. “Have overcome” means have conquered and remain victorious. The evil one is Satan (5:18–19). Young believers are in the thick of battle, and they have won by Christ’s victory (4:4; 5:4–5; John 16:33).

Children. A different word from verse 12 (paidia), suggesting those newer in faith. Their knowledge is the simplest and most precious: God as Father (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). The newest believer, who could not explain a single doctrine, knows the one thing the false teachers with all their learning did not: that the God of the universe is his Father. The one who has walked with him fifty years has not exhausted him, and the one who met him last week is not kept at a distance.

Which group am I in? Probably more than one, and it does not matter much. If you are new, you are not second-class: you know the Father, which is the heart of everything. If you are in the thick of the fight, you have overcome, even on days when it does not feel like it. If you have walked with Christ for decades, the goal is not to retire but to know him more deeply still. And every church needs all three. Older believers should seek out younger ones to encourage, and the young should seek out the fathers to learn from.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers, again. The blessing is said twice, and to the fathers John adds nothing new. What could be added to knowing the eternal Son?

The word of God abides in you. This is the source of the young men’s strength: God’s word dwelling in them (John 15:7; Colossians 3:16; Psalm 119:11). The word is not the reward of strength but its cause. Jesus overcame Satan in the wilderness by quoting Scripture (Matthew 4:1–11), three times, all from Deuteronomy. The eternal Word defended himself with the written word.

You have overcome the evil one. Strength through the word leads to victory over Satan (Ephesians 6:17). Scripture is not information about spiritual warfare; it is the weapon itself, the sword of the Spirit.

How does the word actually make me strong? Not by magic, but by changing what you believe in the moment of temptation. Every temptation is a lie: this will satisfy you, God is holding out on you, no one will know, you cannot help it. The word that abides in you answers the lie with the truth, as Jesus answered with written words. That only works if the word is already inside you, read, remembered and believed, before the moment comes. And if reading is hard for you, listen to Scripture read aloud, sing it, and learn a few verses well. A small sword in the hand is better than a large one left in the cupboard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — Do Not Love the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world John forbids us to love is not God’s creation but human society organised against God. He names its three roots, the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life, and gives the reason: the world is passing away, but whoever does God’s will abides for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
Do Not Love the World

The desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life are not from the Father. The world is passing away; whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Wealth and religion were on public display in the cities of Asia.

Now: Receive created things as gifts, but enthrone none of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not love the world. The tense speaks of a settled affection: do not give the world your heart. The world here is not the created earth, which is good (Genesis 1:31), or the people of the world, whom God loves (John 3:16), but human society organised apart from and against God, with its values, desires and priorities (James 4:4; 1 John 5:19).

The same word, two loves. “God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16). “Do not love the world.” The difference is not the word but the direction. God loves the world as a rescuer loves a drowning man: to save it. We are forbidden to love it as the drowning man loves the current: to be carried by it.

Or the things in the world. The things it values and offers: possessions, pleasures, status, power, when sought as ends in themselves, in place of God.

The love of the Father. This means love for the Father. No one can give his first loyalty to both (Matthew 6:24). Everything in the world may be received and enjoyed as God’s gift, but nothing in it may be enthroned as the heart’s supreme good.

What the world did with the Son. To see what the world is, watch what it did with the Son: it did not know him (John 1:10), it hated him without a cause (John 15:25), and it nailed him to a cross. To love the world is to take the side of those who crucified the Son. And the cross is also the cure: by it, Paul said, the world had been crucified to him, and he to the world (Galatians 6:14). A heart that has seen the Son of God die for it finds the world’s prizes losing their shine. He did not ask us to give up the world and get nothing; he gave us himself.

How do I know if I love the world? Is it wrong to enjoy films, sport or nice things? Enjoying good things is not worldliness; God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). The question is what rules the heart. Some tests: what do you think about when your mind is free? What could you not bear to lose? What makes you envious? What do you spend on most gladly? Would you give it up at once if God asked? Do you laugh at what dishonours him? Does it make you want God less? Worldliness is not a list of activities but a direction of love. Anything, even good things, becomes worldly when it replaces the Father. If these questions show you a strong pull toward the world, that alone does not prove you have no love for the Father: believers feel both loves, and the struggle to put the Father first is itself his work in you.

In everyday life. Name the thing the world offers that most tempts your heart. The next time you want it badly, stop and thank God for something you already have in him. Love is retrained by gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all that is in the world. John traces the world’s system to three streams, which between them water every temptation the world offers.

The desires of the flesh. Flesh here is sinful human nature, and these are cravings for physical gratification: sexual immorality, gluttony, drunkenness, laziness, comfort above all. The world treats appetite as king: if the body wants it, that settles it.

The desires of the eyes. These are cravings aroused by what we see: covetousness, greed, envy, materialism, pornography. The eyes lead the heart (Genesis 3:6; Joshua 7:21; 2 Samuel 11:2). Achan saw, coveted and took; David saw from the roof and sent. And we carry screens built by brilliant people to make the eyes want.

The pride of life. The word for pride (alazoneia, as in James 4:16) belongs with the word for a braggart, the travelling pedlar who promised more than he could deliver. Life here means livelihood: this is arrogance about what one has or does, the boasting of self-sufficiency, the person who needs no God because he has his own resources.

The oldest temptation. Many commentators, Augustine among them, have seen the same three in Eden. The fruit was good for food (the flesh), a delight to the eyes (the eyes), and desirable to make one wise (pride) (Genesis 3:6). And in Jesus’ temptation: bread (the flesh), the kingdoms of the world shown in a moment (the eyes), and throwing himself from the temple (pride) (Luke 4:1–13). The world’s system is very old, and so is its remedy. The first Adam fell at all three points in a garden. The last Adam met all three in a wilderness and did not fall.

Not from the Father. God made us able to enjoy, to see and to achieve, and he made those abilities to serve him. Sin has bent them towards self, and these three desires are the result.

Are sexual desire and ambition the desires of the flesh and pride of life? Not in themselves. Sexual desire is God’s good gift for marriage (Genesis 2:24; Proverbs 5:18–19), and wanting to work hard and do well can be obedience (Colossians 3:23). They become the desires of the flesh and the pride of life when they rule: when desire demands satisfaction outside God’s design, or ambition wants glory for self rather than for God. The test is the master. Hunger is good; gluttony is hunger on the throne. Excellence is good; pride is excellence worshipped.

verseByVerse.quote: And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world is passing away. As in verse 8, it is already in motion. To love the world is to invest in a structure already collapsing (1 Corinthians 7:31). And John adds: along with its desires. Not only the things pass, but the wanting of them. The appetite that seemed so urgent at twenty is gone at eighty, and what it sacrificed for is gone with it.

Every empire passes. When John wrote, the Roman Empire looked eternal. Its roads ran from Britain to Syria; its emperors were worshipped as gods. Today tourists photograph its ruins. Every great city, every fashion, every fortune, every name in lights will be the same. A man who builds his life on any of them is building a house on a tide.

Whoever does the will of God. Doing the will of God is living in obedience (Matthew 7:21; 12:50). Not that obedience earns eternal life. Those who do God’s will already share that life, and they will last when the world is gone.

The one who did the will of God. There has been one man of whom this sentence is perfectly true. Jesus came saying, “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7), and he did it all the way to the cross; by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:10). The believer who does God’s will abides for ever, not because his obedience can outlast the world, but because he is joined to the Son who did the Father’s will perfectly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the world will be annihilated. The present order will be renewed (2 Peter 3:13). What passes away is the world as a rebellious system.

How do I know what the will of God is? Mostly, by reading it. God’s will in John’s sense is not a hidden plan for your career that you must decode, but his revealed will in Scripture: to believe in his Son and love one another (3:23), to be holy (1 Thessalonians 4:3), to give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18). For decisions Scripture does not settle, such as which job or which house, obey what is clear, pray for wisdom (James 1:5), seek counsel, and then choose freely within his commands. A believer who is doing the revealed will of God is in the will of God, whichever good option he picks.

In everyday life. A calendar and a bank statement are quiet confessions of what we think will last. Most of what fills them is right and good. But it is worth asking now and then how much of a month went into God’s word and God’s people, the things that will outlast the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Antichrists, Apostasy, and the Anointing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Antichrists have left the church, denying the Father and the Son. Their leaving showed that they never belonged, and ordinary believers have the anointing of the Holy Spirit, who keeps them in the truth they heard from the beginning, and so in the Son and the Father.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Anointing

Those who left showed that they were never of the church. Every believer has the anointing of the Spirit, who keeps him in the truth he heard from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers offered superior knowledge.

Now: Beware any teaching that says Scripture, the Spirit and the church are not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children, it is the last hour. The last hour is the final period of history before Christ’s return, which began with his first coming (Hebrews 1:2; 1 Peter 1:20). The clock of history has struck the last hour, and every hour since has been part of it.

Antichrist is coming. The word appears in the Bible only in John’s letters (2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7). The prefix anti carries two senses at once: against, an opponent, and in place of, a counterfeit substitute. The antichrist is both: an adversary of Christ and a false usurper who offers himself as an alternative Christ. The readers had been taught that a great opponent of Christ would come at the end (Mark 13:22; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–12).

Many antichrists. Before the final antichrist, many smaller antichrists appear: all who deny Christ, especially false teachers within the church (vv. 19, 22). And the shock: they are not pagan outsiders but former insiders. The enemy had sung in their meetings and eaten at their tables.

Therefore we know. Their presence is evidence that the final period has begun. What frightened the church becomes a sign that God’s timetable is running as foretold. The true Christ is not anxious about the counterfeits. He has already won, and the last hour is simply the time he is taking to gather his own.

Where Christians differ: who is the antichrist? Some identify the antichrist with a specific future world ruler who will appear during a seven-year tribulation after a secret rapture; the Reformers often identified the papacy as the antichrist; others see the antichrist as a principle only, not a person. Each view is held by believers who love Christ’s appearing, and the hope they share, his personal and visible return, is far larger than their disagreement. This commentary’s view: John teaches both: the spirit of antichrist is present throughout the church age in the many who deny Christ, and Scripture also foretells a final, personal climax of opposition before Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8). This fits the amillennial view, which reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a picture of the whole present age, with Christ reigning now, rather than as a later earthly reign; this commentary holds it because the New Testament speaks of one return of Christ, bringing resurrection and judgment together (John 5:28–29), though many faithful Christians read the prophecies differently. On that view, throughout the age between Christ’s comings, antichrists arise, culminating in a final great deceiver whom Christ will destroy at his single, visible return. Believers should not speculate about identities but test every spirit by its confession of Christ (4:1–3).

What it does not mean. “Last hour” does not mean John expected the end within months. It describes the kind of time we live in: the final stage before Christ returns. Nor should believers be fearful; antichrists cannot snatch Christ’s sheep (John 10:28).

Is it right to call a false teacher antichrist today? John did, so the category is real, and it is defined by the denial of Christ’s true identity (v. 22; 4:3), not by politics, personality or how much we dislike someone. Any teaching that denies that Jesus is the eternal Son of God who came in the flesh, died and rose, is of the spirit of antichrist, however warm its tone. But the label is not for throwing at fellow Christians with whom we disagree about secondary matters, nor at every leader we fear. Use it seldom, carefully, and with sorrow, and always more concerned to protect the sheep than to win the argument.
verseByVerse.note: “Antichrist” appears in the Bible only in John’s letters.

verseByVerse.quote: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went out from us. The false teachers had left the church, perhaps forming a rival group. John does not pretend this was not painful: people they had prayed with were gone, and some were now teaching against what they had once confessed.

But they were not of us. “Of us” here means truly belonging, sharing the same life. Their membership was outward only, and the departure revealed it.

That it might become plain. True believers persevere; the departure of these teachers exposed what had always been true of them. Even apostasy (falling away from the faith) serves the purpose of God, separating what only appeared united.

John had seen it happen at the table. The first man to go out from the apostolic circle went out from the Last Supper. Judas had walked with Jesus for three years; then he took the morsel from Jesus’ hand and went out, and it was night (John 13:30). Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64). Peter fell the same night, more loudly, and came back weeping, because he was one of them; Judas went out, and showed that he never had been. The difference lay not in the size of the sin but in the keeping of the Lord, who had prayed that Peter’s faith would not fail (Luke 22:32).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer fall away and be lost? Arminian Christians hold that true believers can fall away, pointing to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). They hold it out of a desire to take those warnings with full seriousness, and many of them are devoted followers of Christ. This commentary’s view: This verse is one of the clearest statements of the perseverance of the saints. Those who finally depart from Christ and his people show that they were never truly of us, never genuinely regenerated. If they had been, they would have continued. True believers may stumble, backslide and need restoring, but they will not finally fall away, because God keeps them (John 6:37–40; 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). The warnings of Hebrews are real, and they are one of the means God uses to keep his people persevering. This is not a cause for complacency, but for assurance, and for testing ourselves.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone who leaves a particular church is an unbeliever. People move, churches err, and believers sometimes leave for good reasons. John speaks of those who left the apostolic faith and fellowship, denying Christ (v. 22).

Someone I love professed faith and has now walked away. What do I make of it? First, grieve; John did not pretend it was nothing. Then remember that you cannot see the end of the story. Some who wander are true believers in a terrible backslidden season, like Peter after his denial, and they come back. Others, if they never return, will show that they did not truly belong, and that is the sorrow of this verse. You do not have to decide which today. Your part is to pray, to keep loving them, to keep the door open, and to speak the truth when it can be heard. God is able to bring back the lost, and he often does it years later.

Could I be one of those who leave? The people who ask this anxiously are rarely the people in danger of it. The warning is real, and it is meant to keep you close. But the promise is just as real: no one will snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Your perseverance rests on his keeping, not on the strength of your grip. Stay where his grace is given: in his word, at prayer, among his people, at his table. Those are the very means by which he keeps you.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anointed by the Holy One. In contrast with those who left, you have an anointing (chrisma), a word related to Christ, the Anointed One, and to antichrist. The wordplay is unmistakable: the anti-anointed ones have gone; you are the anointed ones of the Anointed One. The anointing is the Holy Spirit, given to all believers (2 Corinthians 1:21–22), by “the Holy One”, who is Christ (John 6:69) or perhaps the Father.

You all have knowledge. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “you know all things” (panta); “you all” (pantes) is better supported. Against the false teachers who claimed knowledge only for an elite, John says every believer has the Spirit and knows the truth (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11).

In the Old Testament, oil was poured on few heads. Prophets, priests and kings were anointed, a handful in each generation. Moses longed for the day when all the LORD’s people would be prophets, and the LORD would put his Spirit on them (Numbers 11:29). Joel promised it (Joel 2:28). Now John says to an ordinary congregation of slaves, tradesmen and widows: you have the anointing, all of you.

Do I need a special experience to have this anointing? No. John says all his readers have it, and he is writing to ordinary believers, not to a spiritual elite. The anointing is the Holy Spirit himself, given to every Christian at conversion (Romans 8:9; Ephesians 1:13). You may not have felt anything dramatic when you came to faith, but if you trust Christ, love him, and find the gospel true and precious, the Spirit is at work in you, for no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). Some believers have vivid experiences and some quiet ones; the anointing is the same.

In everyday life. Do not be intimidated by people who sound more spiritual or more learned than you. You have the same Spirit. Open your Bible today, ask him to teach you, and trust that he will.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because you know it. John writes not to inform the ignorant but to confirm what his readers already know: this is a letter of assurance, not a course in basic Christianity. Most of the Christian life is not learning new things but remembering old ones at the right moment.

No lie is of the truth. Truth and lies have different sources. Because they know the truth, they can recognise lies (John 8:44; 14:6). The false teaching is not a different angle on the same reality; it is incompatible with the truth. Bank clerks are said to learn counterfeit notes not by studying every forgery but by handling the real thing until anything else feels wrong in the hand.

The truth has a face. In John’s writings truth is not first a list of correct statements but a person: Jesus said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), and the false teachers’ lie was a lie about him (v. 22). A believer who has spent years with the Christ of the Gospels may not answer every clever argument, but he knows when the Jesus he is being offered is not the one he loves.

How can I tell truth from a lie when both sides quote the Bible? Ask several questions. Does this teaching agree with the plain meaning of Scripture read in context, or does it depend on one verse twisted away from the rest? Does it exalt Christ as fully God and fully man, the only Saviour, or does it shrink him? Does it agree with what the church has confessed across the centuries, or does it claim that everyone was wrong until now? Does it produce humility, holiness and love, or pride and division? And take it to mature believers and faithful pastors. A lie usually fails at least one of these.

For worship. The Truth once stood on trial. Pilate looked at him and asked what truth is, while the Truth stood in front of him, bound, and was handed over to be crucified on the word of liars (John 18:38). But no lie could keep him in the grave. He rose, and the world’s verdict was overturned by the verdict of God. He is the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14), and he will not let his children be finally deceived.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? “The liar” (ho pseustēs) means the liar above all others, and this is the lie above all lies. “Denies that Jesus is the Christ”: the false teachers apparently separated the human Jesus from the divine Christ, claiming the Christ spirit came on Jesus at his baptism and left before his death (the view associated with Cerinthus). That would leave only a man to die on the cross, and a death that saves no one. To deny that Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah, the eternal Son come in the flesh (4:2), is the ultimate lie. The confession about Christ is not optional theology; it is the load-bearing wall of the gospel.

Denies the Father and the Son. You cannot deny the Son without denying the Father, because the Father is known only through the Son (John 14:6–9). Claims to know God while rejecting Jesus as the Christ are false.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone with a confused view of Jesus is the antichrist. John speaks of a deliberate denial of the apostolic truth about Christ, by those who once knew it.

Who denies that Jesus is the Christ today? Anyone who denies who Jesus really is, whatever words he keeps. Some deny his full deity, making him a created being, a great prophet or a good teacher. Some deny his real humanity or his bodily resurrection. Some keep the name Jesus but empty it of the Christ of Scripture, so that he becomes a symbol of their own values. The test is not whether someone speaks warmly of Jesus but whether he confesses the Jesus of the apostles: the eternal Son of God, truly man, crucified for sin and risen bodily, the only Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who denies the Son has the Father. To have the Father is to possess him, to be in relationship with him. There is no access to the Father apart from the Son (John 5:23; 14:6; Acts 4:12), however sincere the seeker. The Son is not a signpost to the Father that we may alter or remove and still keep the Father; he is the only way the Father is known, loved and reached.

Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also. To confess is to acknowledge publicly, and confessing the Son brings the Father with him. Whoever has the Son has not part of God but all of him: Father and Son together, in the Spirit.

Where Christians differ: can people be saved through other religions? Inclusivists hold that people of other faiths may be saved through Christ without knowing him; pluralists that all religions lead to God. This commentary’s view: John’s statement is absolute: no one who denies the Son has the Father. Salvation is found in Christ alone, received through faith in him (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17). This is why the church must take the gospel to every nation.

What about those who never hear of Christ? Scripture does not give us another way, and we must not invent one. People are not condemned for failing to believe in a Christ they never heard of, but for their sin against the light God has given them in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Infants who die in infancy, who are elect, are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Parents who have buried a little one may entrust that child to a Judge who is both just and very tender, and many Reformed pastors have found good hope for such children in David’s words about his son: “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23). But for everyone who can hear, Paul’s logic stands: “how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard?” (Romans 10:14). That is why we send missionaries, not why we stop.

Is it proud to say that whoever denies the Son has no Father, and Jesus is the only way? Pride would be the right word if Christians had invented the claim or thought themselves better for holding it. But a messenger who passes on a warning he did not write is not arrogant; he would be cruel to keep quiet. Every view excludes something: to say that all religions lead to God is itself to tell Christians, Muslims and Jews that they are wrong about what their own faiths teach. And the Christian way is the one way that leaves no one room for pride. It is not a summit reached by the good but a gift handed to the undeserving, because God came looking for us in his Son (Luke 19:10). No one is in because he was better than anyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. “What you heard from the beginning” is the original apostolic gospel (v. 7). Hold on to it; do not drift to novelties.

You too will abide in the Son and in the Father. The “if” carries a promise: those who hold on to the apostles’ message will go on living in union with God. Holding fast to true teaching is not just a matter of tidy thinking; it is how we hold fast to God (John 8:31; 15:7). The gospel we first believed is not the shallow end of the faith; it is the whole ocean.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we keep ourselves saved by holding onto doctrine through our own strength. God keeps us (5:18), through his word abiding in us.

What if what I heard at the beginning was wrong? From the beginning in John means the apostolic gospel, not whatever you happened to be taught first. Some people were raised on a distorted message: a gospel of works, of prosperity, of fear, or of a Jesus who was merely an example. Abiding in what was heard from the beginning means going back past your own beginning to the apostles’ beginning, the gospel written in the New Testament. If your first teachers were wrong, let Scripture correct them, and you will find yourself not drifting from the faith but arriving at it.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise. He who made it is Christ, and the promise is secured not by the believer’s faithfulness in holding it but by the faithfulness of the one who made it.

Eternal life. Eternal life is not merely endless existence, which the lost also have, in a tragic sense, but the life of the age to come, the life of God himself, knowing the Father and the Son (John 17:3), now and for ever (5:11–13; John 10:28). The life is in the Son (5:11–12), so the false teachers, in leading people away from the Son, lead them away from the life itself. When everything we have known has passed away, we will still be just beginning, and the life that started the day we believed will open out into an eternity of knowing him.

If I have eternal life now, why does it not feel like it? Because eternal life is first a relationship, not a sensation. It is knowing God (John 17:3), and that knowing is real on dull days as well as bright ones. It is like a seed in winter ground: alive, growing roots you cannot see. It shows itself in small ways: a love for God’s word, a hatred of sin, a care for his people, a hope that will not quite die. And the full flowering is still to come. Jesus said whoever believes has eternal life and has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Trust his word over your mood.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are trying to deceive you. The verb means leading astray, and the tense says they are actively trying. It is the word used in “we deceive ourselves” (1:8): fooling ourselves and being fooled by others are the same disease. Naming the threat clearly is an act of pastoral love; it helps the church to resist the false teaching instead of taking it in out of a mistaken kindness.

Words John heard on the Mount of Olives. John was one of the four who asked Jesus privately about the end (Mark 13:3), and the Lord’s first words were a warning: see that no one leads you astray; many will come in my name and lead many astray (Mark 13:5–6). Decades later the old disciple uses the same verb, naming the danger before it strikes.

How do I recognise a deceiver if he seems sincere and kind? Remember that most deceivers are sincere; they have been deceived first (2 Timothy 3:13). Sincerity is not truth, and kindness is not sound teaching. The most dangerous deceptions in the church are usually the ones not identified as deceptions, because they arrive wrapped in spiritual language and appealing sincerity. Watch what is said about Christ, about sin, and about Scripture. Ask whether the teaching draws you to Christ and his people, or to the teacher and his group. Be wary when you are told the church has missed something only this teacher sees. And do not judge alone; take it to faithful pastors.

verseByVerse.quote: But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The anointing abides in you. The Spirit remains permanently (John 14:16–17). He is not a visitor for good meetings only. The same Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation, who overshadowed Mary, who raised Jesus from the dead, has made his home in us to teach us Christ.

No need that anyone should teach you. You do not need the false teachers’ higher knowledge; you already have the Spirit and the apostolic truth.

His anointing teaches you. The Spirit teaches believers, guiding them into the truth (John 14:26; 16:13), not by giving new revelation, but by making the apostles’ message clear to them, confirming it in their hearts, and enabling them to recognise error.

True, and no lie. The Spirit is the Spirit of truth (John 14:17). His teaching is the opposite of the deceivers’.

Abide in him. That is, in Christ. The remedy for every form of false teaching is not winning arguments but staying joined to the Son, kept by the Spirit and holding to the word received from the beginning.

Where Christians differ: does this verse mean believers do not need teachers? Some have used this verse to reject all church teaching, or to claim private revelations from the Spirit. This commentary’s view: John himself is teaching them in this very letter. Christ gave teachers to the church (Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 2:2). John means they do not need the false teachers’ new knowledge, because the Spirit has given them the true knowledge through the apostolic gospel. The Spirit does not give new revelation that contradicts or adds to Scripture; he illuminates Scripture and confirms its truth to the heart. Every claim to Spirit-given teaching must be tested by the apostolic word (4:1–6).

What about when I feel the Spirit has told me something? Test it by Scripture, humbly. The Spirit who inspired the Bible does not contradict it, and he no longer adds to it, since the Bible is complete. He does give believers conviction of sin, assurance, comfort, and wisdom to apply his word, and he guides through his word and through providence. But an inner impression is not a revelation with authority over anyone else, and it can come from our own desires. If a feeling leads you toward something Scripture forbids, it is not the Spirit. If it leads you to obey what Scripture says, follow it gladly, and say “I believe God wants this”, not “God told me”. Christians who believe the gift of prophecy continues today usually agree that any such word must be tested by Scripture and never binds the conscience as Scripture does, and on that shared ground believers on both sides can stand together.

In everyday life. Before you read Scripture today, pray a short prayer for the Spirit to open your eyes (Psalm 119:18). Then read slowly, expecting him to teach you, and write down one thing he shows you about Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — Abide in Him: The Returning King and the Family Likeness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends looking to Christ’s return: remain in him now, so as to meet him with confidence and not shrink from him in shame. Then John opens a theme for the rest of the letter: everyone who practises righteousness shows the family likeness of one born of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Abide in him

Abide in Christ so as to have confidence at his coming. Those born of the righteous God practise righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Christ’s appearing was still ahead.

Now: Live now as someone who will meet him face to face.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abide in him. The call to abide has gathered force through the chapter (vv. 6, 10, 24, 27) and now John gives its final reason: Christ is coming back.

So that when he appears. “Appears” means is revealed, made visible: the same word as 1:2, where the life appeared in the incarnation. He appeared once in humility; he will appear again in glory, visibly and publicly.

We may have confidence. The word for confidence was used of a citizen’s right to speak freely in the assembly, with nothing to fear. Here it is a child running to greet a returning father, not hiding. John includes himself.

Not shrink from him in shame. Coming (parousia) is the word used of a king’s official visit to a city. The shame is not only a punishment imposed from outside. It is the horror anyone must feel on meeting the one whose commands he spent his life ignoring.

Will I be ashamed when he comes because of my sins? Not if you are in him. Your sins were judged at the cross, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The confidence John speaks of is not earned by perfection but rests on abiding: trusting him, staying near him, walking in the light with your sins confessed. There may be things in your life you will wish you had done differently, and some work may be lost (1 Corinthians 3:15). But the believer will meet his Lord as a child meets a father coming home, not as a criminal meets a judge. Live now in the way you will be glad of then.

For worship. He is coming. The one who appeared in a manger will appear in the sky, and for his own it will be the homecoming they have waited for all their lives, when the bridegroom comes for the bride and the king enters his city. Those who have stayed close to him will run to meet him unashamed, because the one they meet is the one who covered all their shame.

verseByVerse.quote: If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you know that he is righteous. “He” is Christ (v. 1) or God the Father, since “born of him” refers to the Father. Righteous means perfectly upright, always doing what is right.

In the flow. This verse closes the call to abide and opens the letter’s next great theme, new birth: obedience, love and right belief are all rooted in having been born of God, as chapter 3 unfolds.

Born of him. To practise righteousness is to do it habitually, and “has been born” means born at a point in the past and still God’s child now. This is the first mention of new birth in 1 John, and the order matters: birth first, righteousness as its evidence. The new birth is a change of nature, not only of status. Children resemble their Father.

The likeness of the Son. John does not stop to say whether the righteous one is the Father or the Son (2:1), because their righteousness is one. The family likeness God is producing in his children is the likeness of his Son, whom he has made the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). When a child of God does what is right, it is the life of the Firstborn showing in a younger brother. His children do not yet look much like him, but they will. He has never yet failed to raise a child to his likeness, and he will finish what he started.

Must I have had a dramatic born-again experience? No. New birth is God’s work, done once, often silently: “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3:8). Some can name the day; many raised in Christian homes cannot remember a time when they did not trust Christ. What matters is not the memory of the birth but the evidence of the life. A man does not prove he was born by remembering his birthday but by being alive. If you trust Christ and are growing, however slowly, in doing what is right, you have been born of him.

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The two words of 2:1–2 look at Christ’s saving work from two sides. As advocate, he represents us before the Father, and he can plead our case because he is righteous. As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation: the wrath of God against our sin was borne at the cross. The atonement was finished once, in history, and Christ goes on pleading it for us now. Together they give the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John’s three tests, obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11) and belief (2:22–23), are not a checklist for earning assurance but signs of new birth, as a doctor looks for signs of life. The question is not whether I have been good enough but whether the Spirit’s fruit is growing in me. And they belong together, because obedience, love and right belief about Jesus grow from the same new life.
2.examples:
Then: The teachers who had left claimed a superior knowledge of God. John answers that by leaving they showed they had never truly belonged (2:19), and that those who remained, perhaps confused and fewer, had the anointing from the Holy One and knew the truth (2:20).

Now: Every generation is offered new spiritualities and new paths to a better self, and the church is tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more current. The gospel does not need updating; it needs to be lived in. We go deeper not by moving beyond the cross but by going further into it.

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.<sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.<sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.<sup>4</sup>Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.<sup>5</sup>You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.<sup>6</sup>No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.<sup>7</sup>Little children, let no one deceive you. 3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens in wonder at the Father’s love, which has made us his children now, with the promise that when Christ appears we shall be like him. That hope makes us pure.

Then John shows what God’s children look like. They do not settle into sin, because God’s seed abides in them and the Son came to destroy the devil’s works. And they love one another in deed, as Christ laid down his life for us. When the heart condemns, God is greater than our heart, and his command gathers everything into one: believe in his Son and love one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Children of God: Now and Not Yet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John stops and points at something astonishing: the Father’s love has made us his children, really and now, though the world does not recognise us any more than it recognised him. What we will be is not yet seen, but when Christ appears we shall be like him, and that hope purifies us now.
verseByVerse.theology:
Children Now, Like Him Then

We are God’s children now; when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. That hope purifies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some claimed they had already arrived.

Now: We become what we behold; set your hope on his appearing.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 John 3 is about the children of God: who they are, how they live, and how they can be sure. The Father’s love makes us his children now, and when Christ appears we will be like him, a hope that purifies (vv. 1–3). Christ appeared to take away sins and destroy the works of the devil, so no one born of God keeps on sinning as a settled practice (vv. 4–10). Love for the brothers, unlike Cain’s hatred, shows that we have passed from death to life, and Christ laying down his life defines it (vv. 11–18). So we can reassure our hearts before God, pray with confidence, and know that he abides in us by the Spirit (vv. 19–24). The chapter begins with the Father’s love and ends with the Father’s Spirit living in us, and everything between is the family likeness.

See what kind of love. “See” is a command to stop and look, a cry of wonder. John is stopping in the road and pointing. The Greek for “what kind of” is used of things out of the ordinary, as when the disciples asked what sort of man even winds and sea obey (Matthew 8:27): this love comes from outside the world. The tense of “has given” means the gift remains: handed over and not taken back.

Called children of God. The word for children means born ones. Not merely adopted (though that is true, Romans 8:15), but born of God (2:29), sharing his nature. Not that we become God, but that he gives us a new heart that begins to love what he loves (Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Peter 1:4). Adoption says we have the legal standing of sons; birth says we have the life of sons. A king might adopt an orphan and give him his name, but he cannot give him his blood. God does both. The God who needs nothing has chosen to have children. He looked at rebels who had run from his house and wasted his gifts, and he did not merely pardon them and send them on their way; he brought them into his family, gave them his name, put his life in them, and seated them at his table. It cost him his only Son, who became a child of man so that the children of men might become children of God.

And so we are. John interrupts himself with the two most important words in the verse. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, omit them; the earliest include them. The calling is not a courtesy title but a fact: we are truly God’s children, now, on the day we read this, with all our failures in plain view.

The world does not know us. Unbelieving humanity did not recognise Jesus as the Son of God (John 1:10–11), and so it does not recognise his family likeness in his children. Our true identity is hidden from the world, as his was.

The prince in the rags. Think of the old stories of a king’s son who travels his father’s kingdom in disguise. No one guesses, and he is no less the prince for it. The day will come when he rides back through the same towns with his father’s banners, and everyone who pushed him aside will know. That is the believer in the world. The Son himself came like that: born in a borrowed stable, a carpenter in a despised town, crucified as a criminal, and the world did not know him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all people are God’s children by nature. All are his creatures, but only those born of him by faith in Christ are his children (John 1:12–13; 8:42–44).

What if I do not feel like a child of God? Then look again at what John says. He does not say, see how you feel. He says, see what love the Father has given. Your sonship rests on his gift, not on your feelings, and the gift was given to those who received his Son and believed in his name (John 1:12). If you trust Christ, you are God’s child on the bad days as fully as on the good. Children do not stop being children when they are sulking, ill or ashamed. Say to yourself what John says: “and so we are”. Then speak to God as Father, even if the word feels strange. The Spirit teaches us to say it (Romans 8:15).

Should I want the world to like me? Wanting to be at peace with people is good (Romans 12:18), and Christians should be the kindest neighbours on the street. But you cannot make being understood by the world your aim, because the world did not understand your Lord. If people misread you because you will not join in their sin, or because you love a Christ they do not know, do not take it as a sign that you have failed. It is the family likeness showing. Be gentle, be honest, and be content to be known by your Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children now. “Now” is the present fact: we are God’s children already. But the best is still to come, and John holds the two together.

Not yet appeared. The full glory of being children is hidden (Romans 8:18–19; Colossians 3:3–4). An acorn is a real oak in the making, but nobody looking at it would guess the tree.

We shall be like him. When he appears is Christ’s return (2:28), and like him means like Christ in his glorified humanity: holy, immortal, with resurrection bodies (Philippians 3:21; 1 Corinthians 15:49; Romans 8:29). We will not become divine, but we will be shaped into his likeness. And John says we know. He does not know what we will look like, but he knows whom we will look like.

We shall see him as he is. This is what the church has called the beatific vision, the sight of God that makes us blessed. Now we see dimly (1 Corinthians 13:12); then face to face (Revelation 22:4; Matthew 5:8). As Moses’ face shone after seeing God’s glory (Exodus 34:29), so seeing Christ will make us like him. The order matters: we do not become like him and then qualify to see him; we see him, and are changed. That sight will accomplish in an instant what a lifetime of the Spirit’s slow work has been working toward. The eyes that have wept at gravesides and strained to read the promises in the dark will look on the face of the Son of God, with nothing between. No mirror, no dimness, no faith struggling to hold on, but sight.

Becoming what we behold. It happens already in a small way. People grow like what they gaze at: children pick up a parent’s laugh; a man who watches cruelty becomes cruel. Paul says that even now, beholding the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The final sight will finish the work. The psalmist saw it from far off: “when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness” (Psalm 17:15).

Will I still be me? Yes, more than you have ever been: the risen Jesus was recognisably himself, and being made like Christ completes everything God made you to be. (See 1 Corinthians 15:37–38 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. When the mirror shows age, weakness or the marks of sin, say: this is not yet what I will be. And spend five minutes today simply looking at Christ in a Gospel passage. It is how the likeness grows.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who thus hopes in him. Literally, has this hope set on him. Biblical hope is not wishful thinking but a sure expectation of what we do not yet see: an anchor, not a guess.

Purifies himself as he is pure. Purifies means makes holy, cleanses, and the tense means keeps purifying. It is the word used of ritual purification before a festival (John 11:55), when pilgrims went up to Jerusalem early to make themselves ready for the Passover. “As he is pure”: Christ’s own purity is the target, not “as pure as humanly possible”. True hope in Christ’s return leads to holy living (2 Peter 3:11–14): what we expect then shapes how we live now.

The bride before the wedding. Think of a bride in the week before her wedding. Nobody needs to tell her to get ready. She is not anxious that the groom will reject her; he has already chosen her. She gets ready because she is going to see him, and she wants to be lovely for him. That is the purifying of this verse: not fear of rejection, but the joy of an approaching meeting. Our hope is not that we will make ourselves fit to meet him, but that he who is pure has promised to make us like him, and he has already begun.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we purify ourselves by our own power. Christ’s blood cleanses (1:7), and the Spirit sanctifies. But we actively cooperate (2 Corinthians 7:1). Nor does it mean we have reached sinlessness (1:8). It means a life turned towards his purity.

How does hoping in Christ’s return actually make me purer? By changing what you want and what you fear. If you truly believe you will see him, soon and face to face, the things that compete with him start to look small, and the sins you cherish start to look like stains on a wedding dress. Hope also gives you staying power: you can say no to a pleasure now because you know a greater joy is coming. Practically, think about his return on purpose. Read the passages about it (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18; Revelation 21–22), sing about it, and ask of each choice whether you would be glad of it when he appears.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Sin, the Devil, and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Read carefully, this passage neither terrifies the true believer nor comforts the false one. John speaks of two families, known by how they live. The Son of God appeared to destroy the devil’s works, and God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives. This is not sinless perfection (1:8–10) but a new direction.
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Birth

God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Claimed spiritual knowledge was being used to excuse sin.

Now: Avoid both errors: tolerating sin as normal, and thinking that any sin proves you are not born again.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who makes a practice of sinning. Literally, the one doing sin, habitually, as a way of life. It is the opposite of practising righteousness (2:29).

In the flow. Verses 4–10 run in two matching waves: sin is lawlessness, Christ appeared to take away sins, so whoever abides in him does not keep on sinning (vv. 4–7); sin is of the devil, the Son appeared to destroy his works, so whoever is born of God cannot keep on sinning (vv. 8–10). Each rests on why Christ came, so the passage is first a description of what his coming does in his people.

Sin is lawlessness. Lawlessness is rebellion against God’s law, defiance. John defines sin first by what it is towards God. Sin is weakness and it does damage, but beneath both it is self-rule: refusing God’s right to command us. And lawlessness is the word Paul uses of “the man of lawlessness” who is revealed before the end (2 Thessalonians 2:3): every sin, however small, shares the spirit of that rebellion.

The small rebellion. We usually measure sin by its damage: a lie that hurt no one seems minor, a theft that was never noticed seems trivial. John measures it by its direction. A child who is told not to touch the fire and touches it has not done much harm if he was not burnt, but he has done something serious: he has decided that his will outranks his father’s. That is every sin. The size of the act may vary; the shape is always the same. It says to God, “I will decide.”

Not my will. Sin says to God, “I will decide.” The whole life of the Son of God said the opposite, and nowhere more plainly than in Gethsemane, with the cup of wrath before him: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). The first Adam reached for the fruit to have his own way; the last Adam bowed to the cross to do his Father’s. Lawlessness is answered not by a better rule but by a perfectly obedient Son, who then took the place of the lawless.

If all sin is lawlessness, are all sins equally bad? All sins are rebellion, and any one of them is enough to condemn us apart from Christ (James 2:10). But Scripture also teaches that some sins are more serious than others: in their effects, in how much the sinner knew, and in the hardness of heart they show (John 19:11; Luke 12:47–48; the Westminster Larger Catechism, question 150). A flash of impatience and a lifetime of cruelty are both sin, but they are not the same. Both truths keep us healthy: we never call any sin small, and we never treat a struggling brother’s weakness as if it were a monster’s crime.

verseByVerse.quote: You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To take away sins. He appeared in his incarnation, and this is why he came. His death for sin was not an afterthought; it was his mission. Take away means carry away, as in John 1:29: “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” Christ came to remove sin: its guilt by his death, its power by his Spirit. To continue in sin contradicts the very purpose of his coming.

The goat into the wilderness. Israel had seen it every year. On the Day of Atonement the high priest laid both hands on the head of a live goat, confessed over it all the sins of the people, and sent it away into the wilderness, carrying their iniquities to a solitary land (Leviticus 16:21–22). The people watched it go until it was out of sight. John the Baptist pointed at Jesus as the Lamb who takes away sin, and the scapegoat shows what taking away means: he carried our sins out of sight, and they are not coming back.

In him there is no sin. Christ is sinless (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). Only the sinless one can bear the sins of others without being destroyed by them; his whole sacrifice rests on his being sinless. A drowning man cannot rescue another drowning man. The holy one, in whom there was no sin, came into a world thick with it, and walked through it untouched, and then took it all on himself. Those united to him cannot be at home in sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ removed all sin from believers instantly. He removed its guilt completely and is removing its presence progressively, and will remove it entirely at his return (v. 2).

How could Jesus be truly tempted if he had no sin? Temptation is not sin; yielding is. Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). He felt hunger, weariness, the pull of escape from suffering, and the devil’s offers were real. In fact he felt the force of temptation more than we do, because he never gave way. A man who gives in after a minute never learns how heavy the pressure can become; Jesus held out to the end. That is why he can sympathise with us. He knows the full weight, and he can help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

In everyday life. When a sin from your past comes back to mind, picture it carried away out of sight, as the goat went into the wilderness. Then refuse to go out into the desert to fetch it back. What Christ has taken away, do not pick up again.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keeps on sinning. The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse. This verse must be read in the light of 1:8–10, or it will produce either false assurance in the person who sins at peace and claims to abide, or false despair in the struggling believer who concludes he cannot be born again. John means the settled direction of a life, not occasional failure.

Has either seen him or known him. Spiritual seeing and knowing are meant. Nobody meets the Lord and goes on exactly as before. Zacchaeus met him, and that same day he was giving half his goods to the poor (Luke 19:8).

I have fought the same sin for years. Am I keeping on sinning? The key word is comfortable. John is describing a person who sins and does not mind, who has made peace with it and stopped fighting. If you hate this sin, confess it, grieve over it and keep fighting it, even after many defeats, you are not the person in this verse. The fight itself is evidence that you have seen him. Paul describes exactly that war in Romans 7, and he was an apostle. Keep fighting with every means God gives: Scripture, prayer, accountability, removing occasions. And keep running to Christ each time you fall. The person who has given up the fight is the one in danger.
verseByVerse.note: The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse (compare 1:8–2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one deceive you. The false teachers taught that one could be righteous without living righteously. John will not allow the separation.

As he is righteous. The one who habitually does right shows that he is righteous, like Christ. Not that doing right makes him righteous (justification is by faith alone), but that doing right shows he has been counted righteous and given a new nature (2:29). And the standard is Christ himself, whose righteousness has been given to us and is now being formed in us.

How can I be righteous and still sin? Because righteous means two things in the Christian life, and both are true of you. Before God’s court you are counted righteous, completely and for ever, because Christ’s righteousness is credited to you (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That never grows or shrinks. And in your life you are being made righteous, gradually, by the Spirit, and that does grow, unevenly. Luther summed it up in a phrase: at the same time righteous and a sinner. The first is the root; the second is the fruit. Rest on the first, and pursue the second.

For worship. Christ is righteous, wholly and without remainder, and he has not kept his righteousness to himself. He has wrapped his people in it as a robe, and then begun to make them what he has declared them to be. The one who clothed us will also fit us to the clothes, until his righteousness is not only on us but in us, and shines out of us for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of the devil. That is, belonging to him. He shares the devil’s character and belongs to his family (John 8:44).

Sinning from the beginning. From the beginning of his rebellion, or from the beginning of human history (Genesis 3). He has been sinning ever since, and those whose lives share that pattern bear his family mark.

To destroy the works of the devil. The verb (lysē) is the word for untying a knot, breaking up a building, releasing a prisoner. Sin, deception, death and bondage: Christ came to undo all of it (Hebrews 2:14; Genesis 3:15), entering the domain the devil thought he owned. He has already won the decisive victory at the cross, and will complete it at his return.

The demolition in the Gospels. Watch the Son of God at work and you see the devil’s works coming apart. A man in the synagogue cried out and the unclean spirit left him. A woman bent for eighteen years, whom Satan had bound, was loosed and stood up straight (Luke 13:16), and the word Jesus uses for “loosed” belongs to the same family as John’s word for “destroy”. A widow’s son on his bier sat up and spoke. Lepers were cleansed and the dead raised. Every miracle was a brick pulled out of the devil’s wall. Then at the cross the foundations went, and Christ went down into death and broke it open from the inside.

If Christ has destroyed the devil’s works, why is there still so much evil? Because the victory is decisive but not yet complete. A war can be won in one battle while fighting goes on for months afterwards; the enemy is beaten but has not yet laid down his arms. Christ disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and he is now dismantling the devil’s works in every life he saves. At his return the demolition will be finished, and the devil will be thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10). So do not fear the devil as though he were Christ’s equal. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Born of God. The tense means has been born and remains so. The new birth happens once, but it is not a past event left behind; the divine life it gave goes on working in the one it has entered.

God’s seed abides in him. The seed (sperma) is God’s life implanted in the believer at the new birth: his nature (2 Peter 1:4), the Holy Spirit, or the word of God (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18). Probably the divine life itself, given through the word by the Spirit, and it remains. A seed planted does not stay a seed; it grows, pushes through soil, and in the end it bears the likeness of the plant it came from.

He cannot keep on sinning. The verb means continue sinning as a lifestyle. A child of God cannot settle down in sin, because God’s life in him resists it: sin in him is always resisted and never made at home. This is also a promise of perseverance: the seed remains. The seed of God in the weakest believer is stronger than all the sin that remains in him, and on the last day it will flower into the full likeness of his Son.

Kept by the one born of God. Why does the seed remain? John answers near the end of the letter: “everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him” (5:18). The one who protects there is most naturally the Son, born of God in a unique and eternal sense. The seed does not survive because the soil is good; it survives because the Son of God stands guard over it. The perseverance of the child rests on the faithfulness of the eternal Son.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach sinless perfection? Some read cannot sin as teaching that a born-again person is incapable of sinning at all, or that sinless perfection is possible. This commentary’s view: John has already said that anyone who claims to be sinless is deceived (1:8, 10), and he provides for believers who sin (2:1). The present tense verbs in chapter 3 indicate habitual practice. A child of God cannot continue in a settled lifestyle of unrepented sin, because God’s seed in him makes it impossible. He may fall, but he will not stay down. He will be grieved, convicted and restored. This is the Reformed doctrine of perseverance (those truly born of God will be kept to the end) and of progressive sanctification (growth in holiness through life).

What about a believer who falls into serious sin, like David? David committed adultery and arranged a murder, and for months he seems to have covered it up. Scripture does not soften it. But God did not leave him there: he sent Nathan, and David was broken, confessed, and wrote Psalm 51. That is what the seed does. It does not stop a believer from falling, sometimes terribly, but it will not let him stay at peace in the mud. If you have fallen badly, the misery you feel is not proof that you are lost; it may be the seed at work. Come back the way David came: honestly, quickly, to the God of steadfast love.

In everyday life. When you sin today, pay attention to the discomfort that follows: the unease, the loss of joy in prayer, the desire to put it right. Do not drown it out. Thank God for it, because it is the seed refusing to let you settle, and follow where it leads, back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two families. There are only two. Every person belongs to one or the other (John 8:42–47). John allows no neutral ground.

Righteousness and love. Here the two tests meet: righteousness (vv. 4–10) and love, which John develops next (vv. 11–18). They are two aspects of the same life: love is the heart of righteousness (Romans 13:8–10).

The Son who remains in the house. It was Jesus who first spoke of the devil as a father, to religious men who were trying to kill him (John 8:44). In the same conversation he told them how anyone moves from one family to the other: “The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:35–36). No one changes families by trying harder. The Son, who belongs in the Father’s house by right, brings slaves in with him and makes them sons.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can always tell with certainty who is a child of God by outward observation. God alone knows the heart. But the general pattern of a life reveals its family.

Are there really only two families? What about decent people who are not Christians? Scripture recognises that unbelievers can be kind, honest and brave; God restrains evil and gives common gifts to all (Matthew 5:45; Romans 2:14–15). We should honour such goodness and thank God for it. But John is asking a deeper question: not whether a person does good things, but to whom he belongs. Jesus said the same to very religious men (John 8:44). Outward decency does not make anyone a child of God; only new birth does (John 3:3). That is not an insult to our neighbours but the reason we must tell them about Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — Love One Another: The Cain Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John brings love down to earth: the brother in front of you. He starts with Cain, who hated his brother because Abel was righteous, and that explains why the world hates believers. Then he defines love by the cross, which obliges us to love the same way, starting with an open hand to a brother in need.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love Defined by the Cross

Cain hated his brother; Christ laid down his life for us. By this we know love, and we ought to lay down our lives for one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The world’s hatred was not to surprise the church.

Now: Love in deed and truth: an open hand to a brother in need.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message from the beginning. The first message (1:5) was that God is light; the second, that we love one another. “From the beginning” (2:7) means this is nothing new. The command to love is not advanced teaching for the mature but the apostles’ message itself, which the false teachers had quietly left behind.

Love one another. The tense means keep loving. This is Jesus’ new commandment (John 13:34–35; 15:12, 17). It is what the gospel produces, and Jesus said it would be the badge by which the world would know his disciples: not their buildings or their size, but their love for one another.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love only for believers. Christians love all people, even enemies (Matthew 5:44). But love for the family of God is a special mark of belonging to it.

Do I have to like every Christian? No, but you must love every Christian, and the two are not the same. Liking is about natural affinity: shared tastes, easy conversation, a sense of humour that fits yours. You will have that with some believers and not with others, and that is no sin. Love is a settled will for another’s good, shown in action, and it is commanded. You can love a brother you find tiresome by praying for him, helping him, defending his name, welcoming him, and forgiving him. Often, over years, liking follows. Even when it does not, love has done its work.

verseByVerse.quote: We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not like Cain. Cain is the first example of hatred in Scripture (Genesis 4:1–16). His was not a crime of sudden passion. It showed what he was: one of the evil one’s family (v. 10). The first child born in the world became the first murderer. The second child born in the world became the first martyr.

Murdered his brother. The verb (esphaxen) means slaughtered, the word used of sacrificial animals, and the word used in Revelation of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6). Abel was slaughtered by hatred; the Lamb was slaughtered by hatred, and for haters.
