And why did he murder him? “Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.” Cain was not provoked by Abel’s wrongdoing, but by his righteousness. God accepted Abel’s offering, which exposed Cain’s evil heart (Genesis 4:4–7; Hebrews 11:4). Evil hates good because good exposes it (John 3:19–20). Righteousness does not have to speak to accuse; its existence is accusation enough to those committed to evil. This explains why the world hates believers (v. 13): those who have chosen darkness feel a righteous life as a rebuke, and their natural response is to put out the light.

God’s warning to Cain. Before the murder, God came to Cain and spoke to him, gently. Why are you angry? If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is contrary to you, but you must rule over it (Genesis 4:6–7). God saw the hatred while it was still a feeling and offered a way out. Cain went to the field instead. Hatred almost always gets a warning, and the warning almost always comes early.

Why did God accept Abel’s offering and not Cain’s? Scripture’s own answer is faith: “By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain” (Hebrews 11:4). The difference was not first in the gift but in the heart. Abel brought the firstborn of his flock and the fat portions, the best, in trust; Cain brought some of the fruit of the ground, and his life showed that his heart was not right with God (Genesis 4:3–5, 7). God looks at the person before the offering. That is why our worship is acceptable only through faith in Christ, the better sacrifice, whose blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24).

In everyday life. Is there someone whose goodness makes you resentful: the colleague who is more conscientious, the sibling who visits your parents more, the Christian whose prayers sound more real? Confess it, and pray for them instead. You are accepted in Christ, the better sacrifice, so another’s goodness takes nothing from you.

For worship. Cain asked whether he was his brother’s keeper, with his brother’s blood still on the ground (Genesis 4:9). There is a Brother who never asked it. The firstborn Son of God took his brothers’ keeping on himself at the cost of his life; when they turned on him he did not curse them but died for them. The first brother killed because he hated righteousness; this Brother gives his righteousness away to the unrighteous. In his family hatred is answered with blood that turns enemies into brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be surprised. As in 1 Peter 4:12, the world’s hatred of genuine believers is not a sign of God’s disfavour or Christian failure; it is a consequence of being in the right family.

That the world hates you. As Cain hated Abel, the world hates the righteous. Jesus warned of it: “If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you” (John 15:18–20; 17:14). We are not to hit back, which is Cain’s way; nor to blend in until there is no difference left; nor to pity ourselves. If you meet coldness or loss for Christ’s sake, pray for the one who caused it, by name, and look for one way to do him good.

The first centuries. The early Christians knew this verse in their bodies. In John’s lifetime and for generations after, they were accused of atheism because they would not worship the emperor, of cannibalism because they spoke of eating Christ’s body, and of hatred of the human race because they kept apart from the temples and the games. Tertullian complained that if the Tiber flooded or the Nile failed to rise, the cry went up at once: “The Christians to the lion!” They were not surprised. They had been told.

What if the world does not hate me? Does that mean I am compromised? Not necessarily. In many places and seasons God gives his people favour, as Joseph found in Egypt and the early church found with all the people (Acts 2:47). Many unbelievers respect a kind and honest Christian. But ask honestly: do people around me know I follow Christ? Have I ever said something about him that cost me? Is there any point at which my life is clearly different from theirs? If the answer is no, the peace may be the peace of silence. If the answer is yes and they still treat you well, thank God for it and use it for the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Passed out of death into life. The verb means crossed over, migrated, and the tense means have passed and remain. It echoes Jesus: whoever hears and believes has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Conversion is a crossing of the frontier from death to life (Ephesians 2:1–5). He brought us across the border from the land of death into the country of life, and he did it by going there himself: the Son of God crossed into death for us and came back out with the keys.

Because we love the brothers. Love is the evidence, not the cause. A doctor checks for a pulse not to make the patient alive but to find out whether he is.

Abides in death. Without love, there is no evidence of new life. Death and life are not only where a person will end up; they are where he lives now.

I find some Christians hard to love. Does that mean I have not passed into life? No. The question is not whether loving is easy for you but whether love is there at all: a real concern for God’s people, a desire to be with them, a gladness at their good, a grief at their harm. Struggling to love a particular brother is part of the Christian life; refusing to love God’s people as such, despising them and wanting nothing to do with them, would be the alarming sign. Mark the fact that you are troubled by your lack of love. That trouble itself comes from the new life. Ask God to enlarge it.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A murderer. The word (anthrōpoktonos) means man-killer. Hatred is the root from which murder grows, as Jesus taught (Matthew 5:21–22). Every murder in history was first a hatred somebody did not deal with.

No murderer has eternal life. Eternal life and settled hatred cannot coexist. This is not a threat against a struggling believer who sometimes feels anger, but a diagnosis of a life marked by settled, unchallenged, unrepented hatred.

The man-killer and the life-giver. John’s word for murderer is the one Jesus used of the devil: “He was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:44). Opposite him stands the one who came to give the life that hatred shuts out: “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). Hatred makes a man resemble the devil; eternal life is the life of Christ, for “whoever has the Son has life” (5:12). To nurse hatred is to keep the devil’s likeness while claiming the Son’s life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a murderer cannot be saved. Paul was complicit in murder (Acts 8:1; 22:20) and was forgiven. It means that a person who lives in unrepented hatred does not have eternal life. Repentance and faith bring forgiveness for any sin.

Is anger always hatred? No. Scripture says, “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). There is a righteous anger at injustice and cruelty, which Jesus himself showed (Mark 3:5). Anger becomes hatred when it settles in and turns personal: when you want the other person harmed rather than put right, when you nurse it, rehearse it, and refuse to forgive. Ask: do I want this person restored or destroyed? Would I be glad if God blessed him? The test of the sunset is wise: deal with anger before it has time to harden.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we know love. The supreme definition of love is not a feeling or a theory, but an event: the cross. We do not bring our own definition of love to the cross and admire how well it fits; the cross defines love for us. There the Son of God, who owed us nothing, laid down his life for people who owed him everything.

He laid down his life. The phrase Jesus used of the Good Shepherd (John 10:11, 15, 17–18): no one took his life from him; he laid it down of his own accord, and on the third day took it up again. “For us” means in our place. Christ died the death we deserved.

We ought to lay down our lives. Ought means we owe it, as debtors. The same verb is now applied to the believer. Not that our deaths atone, but that we should be willing to sacrifice everything, even life itself, for fellow believers (John 15:12–13). Usually this means daily, practical self-giving (v. 17); sometimes it means literal death, as with martyrs.

The plague in Alexandria. In the third century, when a terrible epidemic struck Alexandria, Bishop Dionysius wrote that while the pagans pushed the sick out of their houses and fled from their dearest, the Christians stayed. They nursed the dying, Christian and pagan alike, washed the bodies of the dead and buried them, and many caught the disease and died themselves. He said they took the sickness of their neighbours on themselves, and he counted those who died that way as martyrs. They had learned what love is from the cross.

Does laying down my life mean I must never say no, even to someone who mistreats me? No. Christ laid down his life to save, not to enable evil. Love wills the good of the other, and sometimes that means saying no, setting limits, confronting sin, or getting out of danger. Self-sacrifice for a brother in need is commanded; submitting to abuse is not what this verse means, and abuse must never be tolerated in a home or a church. A wife, a child, or anyone being harmed should seek safety and help, and the church should protect them. Laying down your life is a gift freely given in love, not something taken from you by cruelty.

In everyday life. Laying down your life is usually small: an evening given up, a plan set aside, a cost absorbed quietly. Lay down one such piece of your life on purpose this week, for one particular person.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world’s goods. Literally the life of the world: livelihood, possessions. John moves from the dramatic to the everyday: many will never be asked to die for others, but all are asked to share with the brother in front of them now.

Sees his brother in need. The verb means observes, contemplates: not a passing glance, but a clear awareness of the need. He knows.

Yet closes his heart against him. Literally he shuts his inward parts against him. The splanchna were the seat of the deepest feelings, and a related word is used of Jesus’ compassion on the crowds. The picture is of a man who feels the stirring of pity and shuts the door on it. Often it is not cruelty but fear: if I give, will I have enough? The heart that clutches its goods is trusting them to keep it safe. The gospel answers that fear with a Father who did not spare his own Son, and who will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32).

How does God’s love abide in him? “God’s love” may be love for God, or the love that comes from God. John’s question answers itself: it does not. Love that refuses to help is not God’s love (James 2:15–16). The love defined by the cross is not a feeling that remains private and internal; it must pass through the hands, the wallet, the time, the presence.

How much should I give, and must I help everyone? Scripture does not set a figure for this, but it sets a direction: open-handed, cheerful, proportionate to what God has given you (2 Corinthians 8:12; 9:7). Your first responsibility is to those nearest: your family (1 Timothy 5:8) and the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). You cannot meet every need in the world, and you need not feel guilty for that. But when God puts a particular brother’s need in front of you and you are able to help, do not close your heart. Help wisely, so that it truly helps, and where you cannot help alone, bring the need to the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not in word or talk. “Talk” is literally “tongue”: saying “I will pray for you” and then doing nothing. Words alone can deceive the speaker, who confuses saying with doing.

In deed and in truth. Real love acts, and it is genuine, not performed for an audience: it is verified by what the hands do, not by what the mouth says.

A towel, not a speech. On his last night Jesus did not lecture his disciples about humble love. He rose from supper, tied a towel round his waist, poured water into a basin and washed their feet, Judas’s among them, and then said: “If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). John was at that table. When he writes “in deed and in truth”, he is remembering wet hands on his own feet, and before the next nightfall the same Lord had loved them in the greatest deed of all.

Is it hypocritical to do loving things when I do not feel love? No; it is obedient. Hypocrisy is pretending to be what you are not in order to be admired. Doing a loving act for someone you do not feel warmly toward, because God commands it, is the opposite: it is love in deed and truth, even when the feelings are absent. Feelings often follow actions. C. S. Lewis advised not to sit waiting for the feeling but to act as if we loved our neighbour, and we would find ourselves coming to love him. And the act itself is real love, because love is first a will for another’s good. Do the deed, and ask God for the heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — Assurance, Prayer, and the Mutual Indwelling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After such a demanding call to love comes the question: what if my heart condemns me? John answers tenderly that God is greater than our heart. Then come the freedom of prayer, a summary of the Christian life in one commandment, and the Spirit who assures us that God lives in us.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Greater than Our Heart

When our heart condemns us, God is greater and knows everything. His commandment is to believe in his Son and to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Assurance rested on love in deed and on the Spirit given to them.

Now: A tender conscience can rest in God’s fuller knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are of the truth. “By this” looks back to loving in deed and truth (v. 18). Practical love for the brothers is part of the ground on which we settle our hearts.

Reassure our heart. The verb means persuade, convince, set at rest. The conscience accuses; a life of real love is evidence on the other side, as a lawyer produces the record of a life to answer a charge.

Whenever our heart condemns us. The verb means knows something against, accuses. John knows there are believers who lie awake rehearsing their failures, who read every warning in Scripture as aimed at them, and who cannot believe that God could be pleased with them.

God is greater than our heart. There are two readings. In the first, God is greater in mercy: he knows everything, including our genuine love and Christ’s atonement, so we can rest even when our hearts accuse us. In the second, God is greater in judgment: if our hearts condemn us, how much more will God, who knows everything. The context (reassurance, v. 19; confidence, v. 21) supports the first. He knows the genuine faith beneath the failures, and that our will is turned towards him though it is not yet wholly clean. The tormented conscience finds rest not by arguing itself into peace but by accepting his verdict. He knows every sin we have committed and every sin we will commit, and he chose us and sent his Son for us anyway. Nothing will ever come to light about us that surprises him or changes his mind.

Peter on the beach. The best commentary on this verse is a morning by the Sea of Galilee. Peter had denied his Lord three times, with curses. Now the risen Jesus asked him three times, “do you love me?” and the third time Peter was grieved, and he did the only thing he could. He did not point to his record; his record was a disaster. He appealed to the Lord’s knowledge: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (John 21:17). That is exactly the movement of this verse: from a condemning heart to the God who knows everything. And Jesus did not argue. He said, “Feed my sheep.”

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should ignore our conscience when it rightly convicts us of sin. We confess and are forgiven (1:9). It means that when our hearts continue to accuse us after confession, God’s verdict outweighs our feelings.

My conscience keeps accusing me about sins I have long confessed. What do I do? First, distinguish conviction from accusation. The Spirit’s conviction is specific, leads to confession, and ends in peace. Accusation is vague or endlessly repetitive, leads to despair, and never ends; it is the voice of the accuser, or of an anxious mind. Once you have confessed a sin and, where possible, put it right, God has forgiven it (1:9), and to keep punishing yourself is not humility but a refusal of his verdict. Answer your heart with this verse: God is greater. Some believers struggle with an over-scrupulous conscience as a real affliction, and it is wise to talk it through with a pastor, and sometimes a doctor too. Christ does not want you tormented.

In everyday life. Write down the accusation, write next to it the verse that answers it (1:9; 2:1–2; Romans 8:1), and read the answer aloud whenever the accusation returns.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
If our heart does not condemn us. The positive side of verse 20: a conscience at rest through confession and Christ’s blood, not because of sinless perfection but because the life is set toward love and light.

We have confidence before God. Confidence means freedom to speak openly: not arrogance, but freedom to approach God as a child approaches a loving father (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19). It is the same word used for confidence at Christ’s coming (2:28) and confidence in prayer (5:14). John does not want his people to feel guilty where there is no cause.

The child in the study. Think of a child who walks into his father’s study while he is working. A servant would knock and wait; a stranger would not be admitted. The child pushes the door open, climbs on his knee and starts talking. He is not being presumptuous. He is being a son. That is the confidence of this verse, and it is meant to be the ordinary posture of a Christian at prayer.

Is not confidence before God presumptuous? It would be if it rested on us. Coming to God on the strength of your own goodness would be presumption. But Scripture commands us to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16), because our great high priest has gone ahead of us and opened the way with his own blood (Hebrews 10:19–22). Holding back in fear is not humility; it treats his blood as insufficient. True humility says, I have nothing to bring, so I come with Christ. That is the boldest and the humblest thing a sinner can do at the same time.

For worship. The Son has always had confidence before his Father. At the tomb of Lazarus he lifted his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me” (John 11:41–42). That freedom is his by nature, and he has shared it with us: by the Spirit he has made his home in us, and we pray in his name, so that the Father who always hears the Son hears his brothers and sisters in him. The Father has never once turned his Son away, and he will not turn away those who come in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever we ask we receive. The tense means keep receiving. A sweeping promise (John 14:13–14; 15:7; 16:23–24), qualified by 5:14: if we ask according to his will.

Because we keep his commandments. Not that obedience earns answered prayer, but that obedient children ask according to their Father’s will, and their prayers align with what pleases him (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; James 5:16). This is not a bargain, so much obedience for so many answers, but a matter of being in tune: the person who does what pleases God comes to ask for what pleases God, and God is pleased to give it.

The Son who always pleased him. The phrase “do what pleases him” echoes Jesus’ words about himself: “he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). The perfectly obedient Son is the one whose prayers the Father always hears, and Christians pray in his name. Our obedience is never perfect, and our prayers are not heard because of it: we come in the name of the Son whose perfect obedience is counted as ours. But the more our lives are shaped like his, the more our asking is shaped like his, until we find ourselves praying what he prays.

Why are some of my prayers not answered, even when I am trying to obey? They are answered, but not always with yes. Paul, an obedient apostle, asked three times for his thorn to be removed, and the answer was, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Jesus himself, perfectly obedient, prayed in Gethsemane that the cup might pass, and the answer was the cross, which saved the world. God sometimes says no because he has something better, wait because the time is not yet, or yes in a form we do not recognise. A good father does not give a child everything he asks. Keep asking, keep obeying, and trust that your Father hears.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is his commandment. The word is singular. The commandments of verse 22 are summed up in one commandment with two parts. They are not two duties to be weighed against each other but one response to God, because genuine faith in Christ always produces love for the brothers, and genuine love for the brothers is always grounded in faith in Christ.

Believe in the name. Faith is the first commandment (John 6:29). The name means his person and character, all he is, and “his Son Jesus Christ” is the full confession the false teachers denied (2:22–23). This is the first mention of believing in 1 John, and everything else John has said, about light, obedience, love and the new birth, rests on this.

And love one another. The two great tests of the letter are inseparable. Faith looks up and receives; love looks out and gives.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith and love are equal grounds of salvation. Faith receives salvation; love flows from it (Galatians 5:6).

How can faith be commanded? Is it not a gift? It is both. God commands everyone to repent and believe the gospel (Mark 1:15; Acts 17:30), and the command is real: unbelief is sin, not misfortune (John 3:18; 16:9). Yet no one can believe unless God draws him (John 6:44), and faith is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). The command and the gift meet in the gospel: as Christ is offered and the command is heard, the Spirit gives the faith he commands. Lazarus could not obey the command to come out of the tomb by his own power, but the voice that commanded gave the life to obey. So hear the command, and ask for the gift, and believe.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abides in God, and God in him. Each lives in the other (John 15:4–5): God is not merely alongside us or approving from a distance, but in us, and obedience is the sign of it. Jesus promised it at the Last Supper: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23). The Lord of glory lodges in the obedient heart. He has not merely forgiven us at a distance or promised to receive us one day; he has moved in, and he will never move out.

By the Spirit whom he has given us. This is the first mention of the Holy Spirit by name in 1 John. He is the guarantee of God’s presence in us (2 Corinthians 1:22), known by his work: enabling us to confess Christ (4:2), to love (4:13), and to obey. The Spirit gives inner assurance, bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16), and his fruit gives outward evidence.

In the flow. Because we know God abides in us by the Spirit, John must at once warn that not every spirit is from God (4:1–6), since the false teachers claimed the Spirit too. And the verse gathers up the chapter: obedience, love, a heart at rest and faith all belong to this life of God in us and us in God, which the Spirit makes known.

Can the Spirit leave me? No. Jesus promised that the Father would give another Helper, “to be with you forever” (John 14:16). The Spirit is God’s seal on his people for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30), and a seal is not broken. You can grieve him by sin (Ephesians 4:30), and you may lose for a time the joy and sense of his nearness, as David feared when he prayed “take not your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11). But under the new covenant the Spirit is given to remain. If you have him, you will not lose him. Confess what grieves him, and ask him to restore the joy.

In everyday life. Look for the Spirit’s fingerprints this week: a moment when you found yourself trusting Christ, a love for someone that was not natural to you, a temptation refused, a verse that suddenly lit up. Thank God for each one. They are signs that he lives in you.

3.theology:
Adoption and Transformation. In 3:1–3 John speaks of being born of God and called his children, one of the high points of the New Testament’s teaching on adoption. It is a real change of standing: we share as children in the inheritance of the Son. And it is both present (v. 1) and still to be completed (v. 2). What we will be is not yet seen, but that does not weaken what we already are, and the hope of his appearing purifies the one who holds it.

Love Defined by the Cross. In verse 16 John does not say that love is whatever feels loving. He defines it by one act: the Son laying down his life. The cross is love’s definition, its measure and its demand. A view of love that leaves out the cross will shrink into mere tolerance.
3.examples:
Then: John’s readers had been through the pain of seeing people they loved leave. The temptation in such a time is to turn inward, guard the heart, and love in word only. John points them to the cross as the pattern of what love is, and calls them to love with an openness that made them vulnerable.

Now: Our culture often defines love as acceptance and affirmation. John defines it as sacrifice. The question is not first whether I feel warmly toward my brother but whether I am laying anything down for him.

4.title: Testing the Spirits and the Love of God
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.<sup>2</sup>By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God,<sup>3</sup>and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.<sup>4</sup>Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.<sup>5</sup>They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.<sup>6</sup>We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.<sup>8</sup>Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.<sup>9</sup>In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.<sup>10</sup>In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.<sup>11</sup>Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.<sup>12</sup>No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.<sup>13</sup>By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.<sup>14</sup>And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.<sup>15</sup>Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.<sup>16</sup>So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.<sup>17</sup>By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.<sup>18</sup>There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.<sup>19</sup>We love because he first loved us.<sup>20</sup>If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.<sup>21</sup>And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 begins with a warning and rises to some of the Bible’s plainest teaching on the love of God. The warning: test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out, and the test is whether a teaching confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Then John says twice that God is love (vv. 8, 16), and he never lets it become vague. God’s love is defined by its greatest act, the sending of his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. That love casts out the fear of punishment, and it flows on through us to one another, because he loved us first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Testing the Spirits: Discernment in the Last Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Not every teaching that claims to come from God does. John’s test goes to the heart of the gospel: does the teaching confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? And he ends with confidence, because the one who is in believers is greater than the one in the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing the Spirits

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: False prophets had gone out into the world.

Now: Ask of any teaching whether it confesses the whole Christ: truly God, truly man, crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 John 4 brings together the two great tests: truth about Christ and love. First, test the spirits (vv. 1–6): every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that denies it is the spirit of antichrist; believers have overcome the false prophets, because he who is in them is greater than he who is in the world. Second, love (vv. 7–21). God is love, and he showed it by sending his only Son to be the propitiation for our sins (vv. 8–10). So we love one another, and the invisible God abides in us by his Spirit (vv. 11–16). Perfect love casts out the fear of judgment (vv. 17–18), and whoever loves God must love his brother (vv. 19–21). The chapter says twice that God is love, and each time it ties that sentence to the Son’s coming as a man and to his cross.

Do not believe every spirit. The spirit meant is the spirit behind a prophet or teacher: either the Holy Spirit or a spirit of error (v. 6). John neither doubts everything nor believes whatever he is told. He believes in spirits, which is exactly why he will not believe all of them.

Test the spirits. The verb (dokimazete) was used of testing metal to see whether the silver is real, and the present tense means keep testing. Every teaching, however spiritual it seems, must be tested (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). And the command is plural: discernment is not a gift reserved for leaders but a duty given to every believer.

Many false prophets. They are the false teachers who had left the church (2:19), claiming to speak for God. Jesus warned of them: beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing (Matthew 7:15; 24:11, 24). As John writes, they are travelling the roads between the house churches, and the right response is not panic but testing.

The true Prophet behind the test. A counterfeit exists only because there is a genuine coin. Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him, and that the people must listen to him (Deuteronomy 18:15); Peter announced that Jesus is that Prophet (Acts 3:22–23). In these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and every other voice is weighed against his. That is why John’s test, in the very next verse, is a question about Jesus. In all the noise of the world, the church is listening for one voice, and it is his.

The Bereans. Luke gives the model. When Paul preached in Berea, the Jews there received the word with all eagerness, and examined the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so (Acts 17:11). Look at whom they tested: an apostle. They were not rude to him and not suspicious of him; they were eager. But they checked, and Luke calls them more noble for it. A good teacher is never threatened by a congregation with open Bibles.

How does an ordinary Christian actually test a teacher? You do not need a theology degree. Start with John’s two tests in this chapter: what does he say about Jesus (vv. 2–3), and does he submit to the apostles’ word in Scripture (v. 6)? Then ask: does he handle the Bible honestly, in context? Does his life match his teaching (Matthew 7:16)? Does his message make much of Christ and his cross, or much of himself, money or experience? Does it lead to holiness and love? Read your Bible with him open beside it, and ask your pastor or a mature believer when you are unsure. Testing is not a single event but a habit.

verseByVerse.quote: By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this you know the Spirit of God. The test of the Spirit is what is confessed about Christ. John does not tell them to test the spirits by their power, their feelings, their miracles or their success. He tells them to ask one question: who is Jesus?

Has come in the flesh. To confess is to declare publicly, and the tense means that he came in the flesh and remains in it. The incarnation (the Son of God becoming man) was not a temporary appearance: the eternal Son became a real man, with a real body. The false teachers said the divine Christ only seemed human, or came on the man Jesus for a time (2:22). The Holy Spirit always glorifies Christ and testifies to who he is (John 15:26; 16:14; 1 Corinthians 12:3). The Son who sits on the throne of the universe is still a man, with a man’s face and a man’s scarred hands. He took our nature into the life of God and will never lay it down.

Does not confess Jesus. That is, does not acknowledge Jesus as he truly is, the Christ come in the flesh. A few ancient witnesses, chiefly Latin translations and some church fathers, read instead every spirit that annuls Jesus (lyei, dissolves or separates), that is, separates the human Jesus from the divine Christ. The better-supported reading is “does not confess”. And mark the name: Jesus, the man from Nazareth. The spirit of antichrist does not necessarily deny that there is a Christ; it refuses to confess that the Christ is Jesus.

In the world already. The antichrist spirit (2:18, 22) is already active, working through false teachers. It is a present reality, in John’s time and in ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who mechanically says “Jesus came in the flesh” is from God. The confession must be genuine, with the full meaning of who Jesus is: God the Son, truly incarnate, the Christ who died and rose. Even demons acknowledged Jesus’ identity (Mark 1:24) without being from God.

Why does it matter so much that Jesus came in the flesh? Because everything he did for us depended on it. Only a real man could stand in the place of men, obey the law we broke, and die the death we deserved (Hebrews 2:14–17). Only a real body could rise from a real grave and guarantee ours. Only one who shares our nature can be our high priest who sympathises with our weakness. And only the eternal Son could make that obedience and death of infinite worth. A Christ who only seemed human could only seem to save. That is why the church has fought hard for this truth in every century: deny it, and the gospel dissolves.

In everyday life. Your body matters to God; his Son took one. Thank him today for the flesh he wore: the hands that touched lepers, the feet that walked to Calvary, the side that was pierced. And treat your own body, and others’, as something the Son of God was not ashamed to share.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are from God. “You” is emphatic, in contrast with the false prophets: you belong to God, born of him. After the warning about false prophets and the spirit of antichrist, John does not leave the church in anxious alert; he turns at once to comfort.

And have overcome them. As in 2:13–14, they have conquered and remain victorious. “Them” means the false prophets: the readers had resisted their teaching and stayed faithful.

Greater than he who is in the world. “He who is in you” is God, by his Spirit (3:24). “He who is in the world” is the devil, the ruler of this world (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11), working through the false prophets. The victory does not rest on the believers’ strength or cleverness but on the one who is in them, and every believer, however ordinary or doubting, carries him. The devil still rages, but he rages on a chain, and the chain is held by the one who lives in us.

The stronger man has already entered the house. The victory John announces was won before his readers ever met a false prophet. Jesus said that no one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first binds the strong man (Mark 3:27), and that is what he came to do: the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil (3:8). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15). So when John says you have overcome, he is echoing his Master in the upper room: take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

Elisha’s servant. When the Syrian army surrounded Dothan, Elisha’s servant went out in the morning, saw horses and chariots everywhere, and panicked. Elisha said, “Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” Then he prayed, and the LORD opened the young man’s eyes, and the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15–17). This verse is that prayer answered for every believer. The enemy is real and visible. What is with you is greater, and invisible.

If he who is in me is greater, can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No, not in the sense of being owned or controlled by one. A Christian is indwelt by the Holy Spirit, and the one in him is greater; he has been transferred out of the domain of darkness into the kingdom of God’s Son (Colossians 1:13). The devil can tempt, accuse, deceive and attack believers, and they must resist him (Ephesians 6:11–13; 1 Peter 5:8–9). But he cannot take possession of one who belongs to Christ. If you are troubled by dark thoughts or fears, do not conclude that you are possessed; bring them to Christ, to Scripture, to prayer and to your pastor, and seek medical help where it is needed.

In everyday life. Whatever you face today, remember: the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world. Write the verse on a card and put it where you will see it at the moment you usually feel weakest.

verseByVerse.quote: They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are from the world. The false prophets’ source, values and loyalty are worldly. The world here is human society organised against God. Where the false teachers come from explains both what they say and why they are welcomed.

Therefore they speak from the world. Their teaching is shaped by what the world finds intellectually respectable, emotionally satisfying and socially acceptable. In John’s day that meant a spiritual Christ without the embarrassment of a body or a cross.

The world listens to them. The world welcomes teachers who tell it what it wants to hear, because like recognises like (John 15:19). Popularity with the world is no proof of truth; often it is a warning sign.

He who comes from above. John is echoing what he had recorded about Jesus himself: he who is of the earth speaks in an earthly way, but he who comes from heaven is above all (John 3:31). The false teachers speak from below, so they sound like the world. Christ came from above, so he never did, and that is why the world that applauds its own prophets hated him: it hates me, he said, because I testify about it that its works are evil (John 7:7). The crowd that would have nodded at a bodiless Christ shouted for Barabbas.

Itching ears. Paul described the same market: the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Timothy 4:3). A preacher who offers health and wealth without repentance, a Jesus who affirms everything and asks nothing, a spirituality without sin or judgment, will always find a crowd. The crowd is not the test.

Should churches then avoid being attractive or relevant? Churches should be welcoming, clear and kind, and should speak in language people understand; Paul became all things to all people, that by all means he might save some (1 Corinthians 9:22). There is nothing faithful about being needlessly off-putting. The danger is changing the message to fit the market: softening sin, removing the cross, or promising what Christ never promised. Adapt the packaging freely; never touch the contents. If people are offended by the gospel, that is the gospel’s doing. If they are offended by us, that is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are from God. “We” means John and the apostles, the authoritative witnesses (1:1–3). They are God’s spokesmen.

Whoever knows God listens to us. Those who truly know God recognise and accept the apostolic teaching (John 8:47; 10:27; 18:37). The sheep know the Shepherd’s voice: the sheep follow him, for they know his voice; a stranger they will not follow (John 10:4–5). The person shaped by the Spirit of truth recognises truth when he hears it.

Whoever is not from God does not listen to us. How a person responds to the apostles’ word shows whether he is from God.

The one who hears you hears me. Why should listening to a handful of apostles reveal whether a person knows God? Because Christ put his own voice in their mouths. He told them that the one who hears them hears him (Luke 10:16), and he promised that the Spirit would bring to their remembrance all that he had said and guide them into all the truth (John 14:26; 16:13). The apostolic word is not one religious opinion among many; it is the risen Christ speaking through the men he chose. To receive it is to hear the Shepherd himself.

The Spirit of truth and the spirit of error. The Spirit of truth is the Holy Spirit (John 14:17; 15:26); the spirit of error, or deception, is Satan and his demonic influences. This is the second test: do they accept the apostolic witness? Today that word is preserved in the New Testament, and any teaching that contradicts it comes from the spirit of error.

Is it presumptuous for John to say whoever knows God listens to us? Could not any group say that? Any group could say it, and many have. The difference is who is speaking. John is an eyewitness apostle, commissioned by Christ, writing what became Scripture. No church, pastor or movement today can claim that for itself; we can only point to what the apostles wrote. So the verse does not make any modern group the judge of truth. It makes the apostolic word the judge of every group, including ours. The humble church is the one that keeps sitting under the New Testament, and lets it correct its traditions.

In everyday life. Listen to the apostles this week as you would to a living voice. Read one New Testament letter straight through at a sitting, as its first hearers did, and note one place where it corrects you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — God Is Love: The Source, the Measure, and the Goal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When John says God is love, he does not mean a warm feeling or a tolerant mood. Love is the life the Father, Son and Spirit have shared from eternity, and it has been shown in the sending of the Son as the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we ought to love one another, and when we do, the invisible God is seen in his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Love

Love is from God, and God showed it by sending his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The departing teachers’ knowledge produced schism, not love.

Now: No one has ever seen God; when we love one another, his love is made complete in us.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us love one another. Beloved means loved ones: those who are loved should love. John moves straight from testing teaching to love, and deliberately: sound teaching and love are not two options for two kinds of people but two sides of one life. The church that tests the spirits must also be the church that loves.

Love is from God. All genuine love flows from him, not from our natural warmth. A river does not make its own water. Every mother’s tenderness, every friend’s loyalty, every act of self-giving is a stream that rose in God.

Born of God and knows God. “Whoever loves” means whoever goes on loving, with self-giving love. Love is the fingerprint of the new birth and the evidence of knowing God, not knowledge about him but a real meeting with him.

The commandment from the upper room. When John writes let us love one another, he is repeating what he heard at the Last Supper, on the night Jesus washed his disciples’ feet: a new commandment, that they love one another just as he had loved them (John 13:34). The command came with a measure, and the measure was Christ. The love that is from God did not arrive as an idea; it arrived kneeling with a towel, and by the next afternoon it hung on a cross.

The word the church filled. The Greeks had erōs for desire and philia for friendship; the noun agapē was rare in ordinary Greek. The Christians took the word and filled it with the cross, until it meant the love that gives itself for the undeserving. They had to, because what they had seen was bigger than any word had yet held.

My unbelieving neighbour is kinder than some Christians I know. How can that be? It can be, and it is humbling. God gives common grace to all people: natural affection, a kind temperament, a good upbringing (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). Some unbelievers are naturally gentle, and some Christians are converted from very hard natures and still have far to go. Compare each person with where he started, not with each other. And see what John is describing: not niceness, but love that flows from knowing God through Christ, love that includes loving God himself. That said, your neighbour’s kindness should shame the church into greater love, and your Christian brother’s unkindness should be gently confronted.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does not know God. The tense means has never come to know him. To know the one who is love is to be changed by what he is. John is not measuring how warm you feel or how often you fail at love; he is describing someone in whom God’s love has left no mark at all. A believer who grieves over his coldness is already showing the change.

Because God is love. No sentence in the letter says more in fewer words. John does not merely say that God loves, or that love is one of his qualities among others; love is his very nature. Within the Trinity, the Father, Son and Spirit have eternally loved one another (John 17:24). As God is light (1:5), so God is love, and the two go together: his love is holy, and his holiness is loving.

Why only the Trinity can say this. A god who was a single, solitary person could not be love in himself before creation; there would have been no one to love, and he would need us. The God of the Bible needs nothing. Before the mountains were brought forth, the Father loved the Son and the Son loved the Father in the bond of the Spirit. We were not made because God was lonely, but because his love was so rich he chose to share it. And it is that love which made us, that love which came after us when we ran, that love which hung on the cross, and that love which will hold us for ever.

Where Christians differ: if God is love, can he send anyone to hell? Some argue that a God of love could never punish anyone eternally, and so all will be saved, or the wicked will be annihilated. Those who hold these views often do so out of real concern for God’s goodness, and the question should be faced with tears, not triumph. This commentary’s view: God is love does not mean love is God, or that God’s love overrides his holiness and justice. The same John who wrote that God is love wrote that the wrath of God remains on those who reject the Son (John 3:36) and described the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10–15). John has already said God is light (1:5), holy and just, and he defines love by the cross: God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (v. 10). Propitiation means the turning away of wrath, so God’s love does not cancel his justice; it satisfies it at infinite cost. God’s love is seen supremely at the cross, where he satisfied his own justice by bearing his own wrath in his Son. Love that ignores evil would not be true love. God is love, and God is light; his love is holy love. Those who refuse that love remain under the judgment it was given to remove, and face his just and eternal judgment.

Does God love everyone? Yes, in different ways. God loves all people as his creatures: he gives sun and rain to the just and the unjust, is kind to the ungrateful and the evil, and sincerely calls everyone to repent and believe (Matthew 5:44–45; Luke 6:35; Ezekiel 33:11). That love is real, and every unbeliever has received it every day of his life. But Scripture also speaks of a special, saving love God has for his people, chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4–5; 5:25). You need not solve the mystery to enjoy the love. Anyone who comes to Christ finds that this saving love was set on him from eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Made manifest among us. The claim of verse 8, that God is love, rests on a deed done at a known time and place: in the reign of Augustus, in the town of Bethlehem.

His only Son. Only Son (monogenē) means unique, one of a kind, as in John 1:14, 18; 3:16. It shows what the giving cost: God did not send one of many representatives, but the Son who cannot be replaced. The Father did not send an angel or a prophet or a message; he sent the one he had loved from eternity, into a world that would reject him, to die.

Abraham on the mountain. The phrase reaches back to Moriah. God said to Abraham, take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go up the mountain (Genesis 22:2). Abraham went, and at the last moment God stopped his hand and provided a ram instead. Some two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region, God did what he had not allowed Abraham to do. He took his Son, his only Son, whom he loved, and did not hold back his hand. There was no ram for him. He was the Lamb.

That we might live through him. This life is eternal life, now and for ever (John 3:16; 10:10), and Christ is the means and source of life. We were spiritually dead (3:14; Ephesians 2:1); through him we live. Love descends into the world of the dying and brings life from the only source that has it.

What it does not mean. “Only Son” does not mean the Son was created or had a beginning. The older translation “only begotten” expresses his unique, eternal relationship with the Father, not a beginning in time.

If believers are also sons of God, why is Jesus called the only Son? Because he is Son in a way no one else can be. He is the eternal Son by nature, sharing the Father’s being from all eternity, God from God. We become children of God by grace: by new birth and adoption, through faith in him (John 1:12–13; Galatians 4:4–7). He is the Son; we are sons in the Son. Jesus kept the difference even after the resurrection: I am ascending to my Father and your Father (John 20:17). Ours is a real sonship, and it is entirely borrowed from his.

verseByVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this is love. This is the definition of love, and its direction runs from God to us, not from us to God. The sinner is not at the centre straining upward; God is at the centre, moving downward.

Not that we have loved God. We did not seek God; we were his enemies (Romans 3:11; 5:10). We were loved before we ever loved.

He loved us. God took the initiative, when we were unlovable. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8; Ephesians 2:4–5). He did not love us because we were lovely; we become lovely because he loved us.

To be the propitiation. Propitiation, as in 2:2, is the offering that bears God’s wrath in our place and so removes it. The supreme expression of God’s love is that he himself provided the sacrifice to satisfy his own justice (Romans 3:25–26). This is not an angry Father appeased by a loving Son; it is the loving Father sending his Son. Love and justice meet at the cross. When we were enemies, he loved us; when we had nothing to give, he gave his Son; when wrath was due, he bore it himself.

If the Father loved us already, why did he need a propitiation? Because his love is holy. A judge who loved a guilty man and simply let him go would not be loving; he would be corrupt, and the victims of the crime would be betrayed. God’s love does not ignore justice; it pays it. The propitiation is not what made God love us. It is what his love did, at his own cost, so that he could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The cross is not the Father being persuaded to love; it is the Father loving so much that he bore the cost himself, in the person of his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God so loved us. “If” here means since: John is not doubting it but drawing a conclusion from it. “So” means in this way and to this extent: by sending his Son to be the propitiation (v. 10). It echoes John 3:16.

We also ought. We owe it, as in 3:16. We owe love to others because of the love God has shown us: not to repay God (we never could), but to pass his love on. That love gives us both the duty and the power to love: the love of God poured into our hearts through the Spirit (Romans 5:5) is not only an example to copy but a supply to draw on.

The servant who would not forgive. Jesus told of a servant forgiven a debt so vast it could never have been paid, ten thousand talents, more than a labourer could earn in many lifetimes. He went straight out and seized a fellow servant who owed him a hundred days’ wages and threw him in prison (Matthew 18:23–35). The story is absurd, and that is the point. Once you know what you have been forgiven, every debt owed to you shrinks to its real size.

What the pardon cost. Jesus’ parable does not tell us what it cost the king to cancel the debt. John does: it cost the Father his Son, sent to be the propitiation for our sins (v. 10). That is the force of the little word “so”. The love we owe one another is measured not by the size of our brother’s offence but by the price of our own pardon, paid in the blood of Christ. Only those who have stood at the foot of the cross have the heart to forgive like this.

What if someone has hurt me deeply? Must I love him, and must I trust him again? You must love him, which means forgiving him from the heart, refusing revenge, and wishing and praying for his good (Romans 12:17–21). But forgiveness is not the same as trust, and love is not the same as pretending. Trust is rebuilt slowly, by repentance shown over time. Reconciliation needs both sides. And where someone has been abusive, love does not require you to return to danger; abuse must never be tolerated, and the church should protect the vulnerable. You can forgive a person and still keep a safe distance, report a crime, and let the authorities do their work.

In everyday life. Who is the hardest person in your church to love? God loved you when you were hard to love. Love them this week, in one specific way: a greeting, a prayer, an invitation, a kindness they cannot repay.

verseByVerse.quote: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ever seen God. Seen means beheld, gazed upon, and it is the same statement as John 1:18. God in his essence is invisible (1 Timothy 6:16). John does not boast of visions; he points to a church.

If we love one another, God abides in us. Though God is invisible, his presence shows in his people’s love. When believers love one another across differences of taste and background, God is seen more plainly than any private vision could show him.

In the flow. If God showed his love once by sending his Son (vv. 9–10), where can it be seen now that the Son has returned to the Father? John answers: in a church that loves (v. 12), and by the Spirit he has given (v. 13). In the Gospel the same sentence led to the Son who made the Father known (John 1:18).

His love is perfected in us. Perfected means brought to its goal, as in 2:5. God’s love for us reaches its intended goal when it produces love in us for others.

So that the world may believe. At the table where he had washed their feet, Jesus told his disciples that all people would know they were his disciples by their love for one another (John 13:35), and he prayed that they would be one, so that the world may believe that the Father had sent him (John 17:21). When the world looks at a church that loves, it does not see God’s essence, but it sees the shape of the cross: proud people serving, enemies reconciled, the strong carrying the weak.

What the pagans saw. In the second century the pagan satirist Lucian mocked the Christians for their gullibility, but even he noticed how they rushed to care for any brother in prison, sending food and money and visitors. Tertullian reported the pagans saying of them, see how they love one another. The world could not see God. It could see that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God abides in us only because we love. God abides in us by his Spirit, given at new birth (v. 13). Our love is the evidence of his presence.

If no one has seen God, what about Moses, Isaiah and others who saw him? They saw real appearances of God, his glory shown in a form they could bear: the burning bush, the cloud, the throne high and lifted up. Moses was told plainly, you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live (Exodus 33:20), and he saw only the back of his glory. Many think the appearances of the LORD in the Old Testament were the Son before his incarnation. No one has seen God in his essence. The only God, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known (John 1:18). To see Jesus is to see the Father (John 14:9).

For worship. The invisible God has chosen to be seen. He showed his glory once in his Son, full of grace and truth, and he is painting that likeness now in forgiven sinners who love one another. The portrait is unfinished and the brush strokes are clumsy, but the face is unmistakably his. And the portrait is not the end. The day is coming when his servants will see his face (Revelation 22:4), and the God no one has ever seen will be the light of every eye.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Abiding in Love: Confidence, Fear Cast Out, and the Visible Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Assurance rests on the Spirit God has given (v. 13) and the confession of his Son (v. 15). From that union comes confidence even for the day of judgment, because believers share Christ’s standing. Perfect love casts out the fear of punishment, and love for the invisible God is tested by love for the brother we can see.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear Cast Out

Those who abide in love have confidence for the day of judgment. Perfect love casts out fear, and we love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Confidence rested on union with the Son, not on claimed knowledge.

Now: The brother we can see tests our love for the God we cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We abide in him and he in us. This is mutual indwelling, as in 3:24. We do not deduce that we abide in God from moral achievement or sustained feeling. We know it.

He has given us of his Spirit. Every believer has received the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:9), God’s pledge that we belong to him (2 Corinthians 1:22). His presence is known by his work: enabling us to confess Christ (v. 2), to love (vv. 7, 12), and to cry out to God as Abba, Father (Romans 8:15–16). This is why we can say we know rather than we hope.

Poured out by the exalted Son. The Spirit by whom we know this was not given apart from Christ. John had recorded that the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified (John 7:39); the gift had to wait for the cross, the resurrection and the ascension. At Pentecost Peter explained the sound and the fire: Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, had received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:33). Every believer who knows that he abides in God knows it by a gift bought at Calvary and given from the throne.

The deposit. Paul calls the Spirit the guarantee of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:14), using the word for a deposit paid on a purchase (in modern Greek the same word means an engagement ring). The Spirit in us now is the first instalment of heaven: not a sample that might be withdrawn but a down payment that commits the buyer.

How can I tell the Spirit’s witness from my own wishful thinking? Look at what he produces. The Spirit’s witness is not a voice that says you are saved while leaving your life unchanged. It always comes with his fruit: a heart that confesses Jesus as Lord and Son of God (v. 15), a love for his people (v. 12), a hatred of sin, a desire to obey, and a turning to God as Father (Romans 8:15). Wishful thinking can produce a feeling; it cannot produce a new love for holiness and for Christ. If you see these, however weak, the Spirit is at work, and you may trust his witness.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have seen and testify. We means the apostles, eyewitnesses (1:1–3). “Seen” is the same verb as in verse 12: no one has ever seen God, but we have seen the Son he sent. That is the gospel in brief.

The Saviour of the world. This is the title the Samaritans gave Jesus (John 4:42), and it is rare in the New Testament. “The world” here means people of every nation who come to him in faith. In the Roman world emperors were hailed as saviour and benefactor on coins and inscriptions; John gives the title to its true owner.

The Samaritan village. The first to say it were a town of Samaritans, whom the Jews despised as half-pagan outsiders, brought to Jesus by a woman with five husbands behind her. After two days with him they said to her, we no longer believe because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world. They were people everyone thought were outside his salvation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in the world will be saved. Jesus is the Saviour of the world in that he is the only Saviour for all peoples, and he saves people from every nation (Revelation 5:9). Those who reject him are not saved (John 3:18, 36).

What does he actually save me from? From sin in every dimension. From its guilt: he bore the penalty, so there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). From God’s wrath, which we deserved (1 Thessalonians 1:10). From sin’s power: he breaks its rule and gives us the Spirit to fight it (Romans 6:14). From the devil, who held us captive (Hebrews 2:14–15). From death, which he defeated by rising (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). And one day from sin’s very presence, when we see him and are made like him (3:2). He saves us not only from all that, but for himself: for fellowship with God, which is eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever confesses. This is the true confession, which the false teachers denied (2:22–23; 4:2–3). It is the outward sign that a person abides in God, matching the Spirit’s inward witness in verse 13. To confess him is to entrust oneself to him and to say, with full personal weight: this Jesus is the Son of God. The baby in the manger, the man on the cross, the body in the tomb, the Lord on the throne: one person, the eternal Son.

God abides in him, and he in God. Confessing Christ does not earn this union with God, as a work would; it is the open hand of faith that receives it as a gift.

Peter at Caesarea Philippi. When Peter said, you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, Jesus told him that flesh and blood had not revealed it to him, but his Father in heaven (Matthew 16:16–17). That is the confession of this verse, and it is always a gift. No one says it truly by his own insight. Every time a person confesses Jesus as the Son of God from the heart, heaven has been at work.

Is confession a one-time act, and must it be public? It begins at a point and continues for life. The New Testament expects the first confession to be made openly, and baptism is the appointed way: a believer is baptised on his profession of faith, publicly declaring that he belongs to Christ (Acts 2:41; 8:36–38; Romans 10:9–10). But confession does not stop at the water. It continues in worship, in speaking of Christ to others, and in standing for him when it costs. Jesus said that whoever acknowledges him before men, he will acknowledge before his Father (Matthew 10:32). A secret faith that never confesses is in danger. This commentary holds believer’s baptism because in the New Testament baptism follows a person’s own confession of faith; many faithful Christians baptise the children of believers as a sign of God’s covenant promise, and we honour them as brothers and sisters in Christ.

In everyday life. Look for one opportunity this week to say to someone, simply and without embarrassment, that Jesus is the Son of God. And if you believe but have never been baptised, or are unsure what your baptism meant, speak to your pastor this week.

verseByVerse.quote: So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come to know and to believe. Both verbs mean we have known and believed, and continue to. We know his love because he has shown it (vv. 9–10); we rely on it by faith.

The same two verbs. John had heard these two verbs together before. When many disciples walked away from Jesus, Peter answered for the Twelve: we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God (John 6:69). Now, at the end of a long life, John uses the same pair, in reverse order, and the object has become the love God has for us. The love of God is not known apart from the Son; it is known in him. To believe in God’s love is to put your weight on Christ, and to know it is to have spent a lifetime in his company and found him true.

God is love. Repeated from verse 8, it now explains how God and the believer live in one another: to abide in love is to abide in God, because God and love cannot be separated.

Whoever abides in love. That means living in God’s love, receiving it and showing it. Love is not a virtue we add to our relationship with God; love is the atmosphere in which God himself dwells, and where his love is received and passed on, there God is.

How do I come to know and believe God’s love when I do not feel loved? By looking where John looks: not inward first, but at the cross. Feelings of being loved are affected by temperament, illness, upbringing and circumstances, and they can lie. The fact of God’s love was settled in history, when he sent his Son (v. 10). Read the accounts of the crucifixion slowly and say: this was for me. Rely on it the way you rely on a bridge, by putting your weight on it, not by first feeling confident. Speak it back to God in prayer. And let other believers love you; God often makes his love felt through his people.

verseByVerse.quote: By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love perfected with us. By this refers to abiding in love (v. 16). “Perfected” again means brought to its goal (v. 12); here the goal is confidence on the last day.

Confidence for the day of judgment. Confidence is boldness, as in 2:28 and 3:21, and the day is the final judgment at Christ’s return. Believers can face it without fear.

As he is so also are we. As he is: Christ, now exalted, perfectly loved by the Father and righteous. Not as he was, but as he is: the vindicated, glorified Son, in whom the believer is hidden (Colossians 3:3). “So also are we”: we share his standing, loved as he is loved (John 17:23), and the verdict that belongs to him is shared with those united to him by faith (Romans 8:1). Confidence on the last day is not a reward for the holiest believers; it is given to all who are united to Christ, whom the Father has already declared righteous.

The judgment already passed. For the believer the verdict of that day has already been given publicly, when God raised Jesus from the dead, declaring the one who stood in the believer’s place righteous and his sacrifice accepted. The one who will sit on the throne on that day is the one who died for us. We will be judged by our Saviour.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are as perfect as Christ in character now. It means they share his acceptance and standing with the Father, and are growing in his likeness.

Will believers be judged at all? Yes, but not to determine whether they are saved. Everyone will stand before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), and the lives of believers will be opened: what was done for him will be acknowledged and rewarded, and some work that was worthless will be burned up, though the believer himself is saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). Our works will be shown as the evidence of our faith (Matthew 25:31–40). But the question of condemnation is closed: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). It will be a Father’s welcome, not a court deciding our fate.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no fear in love. Fear here means terror, dread of punishment. Not the reverent fear of God that Scripture commends (Proverbs 1:7; 1 Peter 1:17), but the dread of a criminal before a judge.

Perfect love casts out fear. Casts out is the word used of Jesus casting out demons. When we take in that Christ bore God’s wrath for us (v. 10) and that we share his standing (v. 17), love drives this dread out.

Fear has to do with punishment. Fear expects punishment. But for believers, Christ has borne the punishment (v. 10). The bill has been paid; the creditor has sent the receipt. All the terror that should have been ours fell on the Son in the darkness of Calvary, and he cried out because he was forsaken, so that we never will be. Now the Father’s house is open, and his children come in not cringing but running.

Not perfected in love. Fear of judgment shows that the love that paid the penalty has not yet been fully believed. The cure is not greater willpower but a deeper knowing and believing of his love (v. 16).

Slavish fear and filial fear. The Puritans distinguished a slavish fear from a filial fear, a slave’s fear from a son’s. A slave fears his master’s whip; a son fears grieving his father. The slave wants to get away; the son wants to come close. Love casts out the first and deepens the second. The more you know that God will never punish you, the more you will hate to wound him.

I still fear death and judgment. Does that mean I am not a Christian? No. It means you are not yet perfected in love, which is true of every believer this side of glory. John is describing what love does as it grows, not setting an exam you must pass first. Fear of death is natural, and even Christ was troubled at its approach (John 12:27). The cure is not to scold yourself but to feed on the gospel: Christ died to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Hebrews 2:15). Each time the fear comes, take it to the cross and say, the punishment has been borne. Love is still casting the fear out, and it will finish the job.

verseByVerse.quote: We love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We love because he first loved us. This is the gospel’s logic in six English words. It is probably a statement (we love), not a command (let us love). Some manuscripts add him (we love him, as in the KJV), others God; most likely the original simply says we love, covering love for God and for others.

The echo. Our love for God and for one another is not self-generated virtue or accumulated moral character; it is the echo of a love that reached us first. Augustine, preaching through this letter, made love the mark that tells the children of God from the children of the devil; John adds here where that love comes from. A heart at rest in God’s love begins at last to love. Before we were born, before we sinned, before the world was made, he set his love on us. Every flicker of love we now have for him is the reflection of a fire that has been burning toward us from eternity.

Simon, do you love me? John had watched this verse happen. By a charcoal fire Peter had denied Jesus three times (John 18:18, 25–27); by another charcoal fire on the shore the risen Lord cooked him breakfast and asked him three times, do you love me (John 21:9, 15–17). Peter’s love had failed completely, and Christ came first: he lit the fire, fed the man who had denied him, and restored him. Every Christian’s story has the same order: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and only then did I love him.

Did I choose God, or did he choose me? Both are true, but not in the same way. You really did turn to God and trust Christ; you were not dragged against your will. But your choosing was the fruit of his. You did not choose me, but I chose you, Jesus said (John 15:16), and God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), not because of anything he foresaw in us but because of his own love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). When you came to him, you found he had been coming to you all along. That is not a cause for confusion but for worship, and it means your salvation rests on something stronger than your grip. Scripture’s word for it is election: God’s free choice, made before time began, to save particular sinners in Christ and bring them to faith.

In everyday life. Pride and discouragement often start in the same place: with how much we love God. This verse moves the starting point. On the day you feel pleased with your devotion, and on the day you are ashamed of how little you have, the first word is the same, and it is humbling and glad at once: he loved you first.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is a liar. Another false claim, as in 1:6, 8, 10; 2:4, 6, 9. A claim to love God while hating a fellow believer is not merely inconsistent but impossible.

Whom he has seen. The argument moves from easier to harder: if you cannot love a visible person, how can you love the invisible God? It is easy to love a God you have imagined. It is much harder to love the man who sits in front of you at church, with his irritating habits and disappointing failures, and that is the point.

The brother Christ is not ashamed of. The brother you have seen is not only God’s child; he is Christ’s brother. The Son is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and he said that whatever is done to the least of his brothers is done to him (Matthew 25:40). The difficult man in the next pew is a brother for whom Christ died (1 Corinthians 8:11).
