Hatred of him cannot sit beside love for God, because it despises the one the Son was glad to call family and bought with his own blood.

Can I love God and still struggle to forgive a brother? Yes, for a time; struggling is not the same as hating. Forgiving a deep wound is often a process, not a moment, and believers can be genuinely fighting to forgive while still feeling the pain. What John condemns is settled hatred that refuses to forgive and does not want to. If you are praying for the grace to forgive, asking God to bless the one who hurt you even through gritted teeth, and refusing to take revenge, you are not the liar of this verse. You are a Christian doing one of the hardest things a Christian is asked to do. Keep going.

verseByVerse.quote: And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This commandment we have from him. “From him” means from Christ, or from God. Verse 20 argued that the two loves cannot be separated; now John adds that God has commanded it so.

Must also love his brother. To love God genuinely is to love what God loves, and God loves his children. The chapter began with the command to test the spirits; it ends with the command to love the brothers. The two are not unrelated: the Spirit of truth always produces love, and the spirit of error always, eventually, produces division.

Both loves in one act. The commandment came from Christ, who summed up the whole law as love for God and love for neighbour (Mark 12:29–31), and he did more than command it. On his way out to Gethsemane he said, I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father (John 14:31); and having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (John 13:1). At the cross his love for the Father and his love for his brothers were one act of obedience. The commandment we have from him is the shape of his own life, now being written into ours.

What if loving a brother seems to conflict with loving God? Then love God first, and you will find that this is the truest love for your brother too. If a brother asks you to sin, to lie for him, to join in his wrongdoing, or to approve what God forbids, love for God says no, and so does real love for him, because it seeks his good, not his comfort (Acts 5:29; Matthew 10:37). Loving a brother never requires disobeying God. Usually there is no conflict at all: the God you love commands you to love, and the brother you love is best served by your obedience to God.

For worship. The God who commands both loves is gathering a family in which both will one day be perfect. Here our love for him is faint and our love for one another is patchy, and we fail at the very point where the command presses hardest. But the Son kept the commandment perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours, and by his Spirit he is making us like himself. A day is coming when no brother will be hard to love and no heart will be cold toward the Father, and the whole household of God will fill heaven with a love that never grows cold.

4.theology:
God is Love. The sentence God is love (vv. 8, 16) is often taken to mean that love is God: that whatever we call love must be divine and approved by him. John means the opposite. God defines love, and he defines it at once by an act: the sending of the Son to be the propitiation. That love is not soft but costly, not vague but given flesh and blood, a cross and an empty tomb.

The Expulsion of Fear. In verses 17–18 the doctrine of propitiation becomes comfort. The believer tormented by fear of God’s judgment has not yet fully taken in what the propitiation means: the very wrath he fears has been borne and satisfied in the beloved Son. Perfect love casts out fear not by denying judgment but by pointing to the one who bore it, and God will not demand payment twice.
4.examples:
Then: The church had been shaken by teachers who claimed spiritual authority and a more sophisticated knowledge of God. John’s test is not whether they seem spiritual but whether they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh: a test simple enough for a child and sharp enough to unmask a false spirit.

Now: We love because he first loved us, and that answers much Christian guilt and striving. The Christian life is not a performance of love to earn God’s approval but a response to a love already given and already victorious at the cross. When love runs dry, the answer is not first to try harder but to go back to the source (v. 10).

5.title: Faith that Overcomes, Life that is Sure
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.<sup>2</sup>By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.<sup>3</sup>For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.<sup>4</sup>For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.<sup>5</sup>Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?<sup>6</sup>This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.<sup>7</sup>For there are three that testify:<sup>8</sup>the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.<sup>9</sup>If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.<sup>10</sup>Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.<sup>11</sup>And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.<sup>12</sup>Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.<sup>13</sup>I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.<sup>14</sup>And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.<sup>15</sup>And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.<sup>16</sup>If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that.<sup>17</sup>All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.<sup>18</sup>We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.<sup>19</sup>We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.<sup>20</sup>And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.<sup>21</sup>Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
5.overview:
The last chapter draws the letter’s threads together. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, loves God’s children and overcomes the world, and the victory is faith. God has testified about his Son, and his testimony is this: eternal life is in the Son. “Whoever has the Son has life.”

Then John states his purpose: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Not hope or feel, but know. Those who know may pray with confidence and intercede for a sinning brother. The letter ends with Jesus Christ declared “the true God and eternal life”, and one last command: keep yourselves from idols.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Faith, Love, and the World-Overcoming Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John ties faith, new birth and love together as a single reality. Those who believe that Jesus is the Messiah have been born of God, and they love the Father’s children too. His commands are not a crushing weight, and the faith that overcomes the world is faith in Jesus as the Son of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as the Victory

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God and loves God’s children. Faith in the Son of God overcomes the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ordinary faith in Jesus was being called insufficient.

Now: The faith that overcomes is not heroic; it is trust in the Son of God who has already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 John 5 draws the letter together around faith in the Son of God and the assurance it brings. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God and loves God’s children, and faith overcomes the world (vv. 1–5). The Spirit, the water and the blood testify to Jesus: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son (vv. 6–12). John writes so that believers may know that they have eternal life (v. 13), can pray with confidence, and should pray for a brother who sins (vv. 14–17). The letter closes with three certainties: Christ keeps those born of God; we are from God, while the world lies in the power of the evil one; and the Son of God has come, the true God and eternal life (vv. 18–20). Last word: keep yourselves from idols (v. 21). The letter that began with hands touching the Word of life ends by naming him the true God.

Everyone who believes. “Believes” (pisteuōn) is present tense: keeps believing. “That Jesus is the Christ” is the confession the false teachers denied (2:22). The letter’s three great themes, faith, new birth and love, meet in this single verse.

Has been born of God. “Has been born” (gegennētai) is perfect tense: has been born and remains so. The order matters: the person who now believes has already been born of God, so his believing is the evidence of that birth. Regeneration, the Spirit’s giving of life to the spiritually dead, comes first, and faith follows as its sign, as righteousness and love do in 2:29, 3:9 and 4:7.

Lazarus in the tomb. Jesus stood at the grave and called, “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43). Lazarus came. But nobody imagines that he first decided to come out and then was made alive. He could not hear until he was alive, and the voice that called him gave him the life to answer. A dead man does not cooperate in his own resurrection; he walks out because he has been raised. Every believer in every age is a walking resurrection, a sinner who could not come until God made him alive and then came running.

Whoever has been born of him. “The Father” is literally the one who begot, that is, fathered (ton gennēsanta). It is a family principle: if you love a father, you love his children.

Where Christians differ: does faith cause new birth, or does new birth cause faith? Arminians (Protestants who hold that God’s grace enables everyone to believe but leaves the decision to each person) generally hold that a person believes and is then born again, with faith coming from the person’s free choice enabled by prevenient grace, a grace given beforehand to all that makes choosing possible. Both sides agree that grace comes first and that faith is necessary, and many Arminian believers love Christ deeply. This commentary’s view: The grammar of this verse, and John’s pattern throughout (2:29; 3:9; 4:7), shows that being born of God comes first and produces faith, righteousness and love. Jesus taught that one must be born again to see the kingdom (John 3:3), and that those who believe were born of God (John 1:12–13). Dead sinners cannot believe until God gives them life (Ephesians 2:1–5). This is effectual calling, God’s inward call that does not fail to bring a sinner to life: God regenerates, and the regenerate believe. Faith is truly ours, but it is the fruit of God’s prior work.

If new birth comes before faith, should an unbeliever just wait to be born again? No. The command to everyone is to repent and believe now (Mark 1:15; Acts 17:30), and no one has to wait. God gives new birth through the hearing of the gospel (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18), so the place to be is under the word, and the thing to do is to come to Christ. If you find that you want him, that wanting is itself a sign that God is at work. Do not try to look behind the curtain to see whether you have been born again before you believe. Believe, and you will find that you were.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we know. Earlier, love for others proved love for God (4:20). Now, the reverse: love for God proves love for others is genuine. Each test checks the other.

When we love God. Love for people that ignores God’s commands is not genuine love: sometimes love requires saying no, correcting, or refusing to approve sin, because God commands it.

As I have kept my Father’s commandments. John learned this order from Jesus. In the upper room the Lord said, if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15), and then gave himself as the pattern: if you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love (John 15:10). In the Son, loving the Father, obeying him and laying down his life for the sheep were never apart (John 10:17–18). His obedience was perfect where ours never is, and it is counted to all who are in him (Romans 5:19), so the Father receives their flawed obedience for his sake.

What if a fellow Christian says I am unloving because I will not approve of his sin? Then examine yourself honestly, and then stand firm gently. Ask: have I been harsh, proud or careless in how I spoke? If so, apologise for that. But love does not mean celebrating what God forbids. A friend who watches you walk out onto thin ice and says nothing is not kind. True love keeps the friendship open, speaks the truth with tears rather than contempt, does practical good, and prays. Jesus was the most loving man who ever lived, and he told the woman caught in adultery both that he did not condemn her and that she must go and sin no more (John 8:11, in a passage missing from the earliest manuscripts, as most modern Bibles note).

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The love of God. “The love of God” here means our love for God, and it is not merely emotion but obedience (John 14:15). That is as old as Moses, who joined loving the LORD to keeping his charge, his statutes, his rules and his commandments always (Deuteronomy 11:1).

Not burdensome. “Burdensome” (bareiai) means crushing, like the burdens the Pharisees laid on people (Matthew 23:4). God’s commands are good, they come from a loving Father, and he gives the new heart and Spirit to delight in them (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Psalm 119:35).

Why his yoke is easy. The commandments are not burdensome because Christ has carried the crushing part of them. The law’s curse fell on him: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). What he lays on his people now is not the law as a ladder up to God but his own yoke, and he calls the weary to take it as one who is gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:28–29). The commandments ask no less than before. They are lighter because the one who gives them has already borne their penalty.

The wings of a bird. An old preacher’s image: wings add weight to a bird, and yet they are not a burden; they are what lift it. Take them off to lighten the load, and the bird can no longer fly. God’s commandments are like that for his children. They feel like weight only to those who do not yet know what they are for. To a heart that loves God they are the very means of rising toward him.

Then why does obedience sometimes feel so hard? Because sin still lives in us, and the old nature pulls against the new (Galatians 5:17). The command is not heavy; our resistance makes it feel heavy. Some obedience is hard because it costs: forgiving a deep wrong, giving up a relationship, telling the truth at a price. Jesus himself was in anguish in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33–36). Not burdensome does not mean effortless. It means the command is good, the Father who gives it is kind, and the strength to obey comes with it. When obedience feels like grinding burden, the question is not first “How do I try harder?” but “Is the love of God real and growing in me?” Go back to his love, and the load will lighten.

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Overcomes the world. “Everyone” (pan) is literally “everything”, which puts the weight on the birth from God, not on the kind of person. God’s children are not crushed by the world (2:15–17) but triumph over it, and this is why his commands are not burdensome.

The victory, our faith. “Victory” (nikē) appears only here in the New Testament; it was also the name of the Greek goddess of victory, whose images were probably familiar across the cities of Asia. “Has overcome” points to a victory already won: Christ overcame the world (John 16:33), and we came to share in it when we first believed. He said he had overcome it in the upper room, the night before the world crucified him, and three days later he walked out of the grave to prove it. Faith is the hand that reaches out and holds the one who has already won.

The old man in the arena. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, had been, by early tradition, a disciple of John himself. In about AD 155, as an old man, he was brought into the stadium and the proconsul urged him to swear by the emperor and curse Christ, and he would be released. He answered that for eighty-six years he had served Christ, and Christ had never done him wrong; how could he blaspheme his King who saved him? He was put to death. The crowd had watched faith overcome the world.

I feel defeated by the world, not overcoming it. How is this true of me? Overcoming the world does not mean winning every skirmish or feeling triumphant. It means the world cannot finally have you. It cannot make you stop trusting Christ for good, cannot take your eternal life, cannot separate you from his love (Romans 8:35–39). Every time you turn back to Christ after failing, refuse a temptation, keep believing through grief, or choose obedience over the world’s approval, you are overcoming. Victory is often quiet and looks like perseverance. And your victory rests on his, which was complete when he rose from the dead.

In everyday life. The world rarely presses with a lion and an arena. It presses with a headline that breeds fear, a feed that breeds envy, an office that rewards quiet compromise. Overcoming looks ordinary: an honest answer, a prayer instead of a panic, a refusal to despair. Each is faith sharing in a victory already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is it that overcomes the world. A rhetorical question, and it has exactly one answer. The eternal Son took flesh, fought the world on its own ground, and won.

Except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? Only those who believe that Jesus, the man, is the divine Son of God overcome the world. This is precisely what the false teachers denied (2:22–23; 4:2–3). What overcomes is not faith in general, a vague spirituality or confidence in one’s own spiritual resources, but faith in this person: Jesus, the Son of God, and the work he did. The question shuts out every other way and invites every person: anyone who believes this overcomes; no one who refuses it does.

What if my faith is weak? Does it still overcome? Yes, because it is not the strength of your faith that wins but the strength of the one you trust. A child holding his father’s hand across a busy road is safe not because his grip is strong but because his father’s is. A weak faith in a strong Christ overcomes; a strong faith in a false Christ does not. Jesus spoke of faith like a grain of mustard seed (Matthew 17:20), and a man once cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), and Jesus helped him. Bring the faith you have, and ask him to grow it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Three Witnesses and the Life That Is in the Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under Jewish law a matter was settled by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides three: the Spirit, the water and the blood. The water and the blood are Jesus’ baptism and his death, which mark the beginning and end of his ministry. God’s own testimony is greater than any human testimony, and its content is that eternal life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Three Witnesses

The Spirit, the water and the blood agree: the one who was baptised is the one who died. God has given eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teaching separated the Christ of the baptism from the Jesus of the cross.

Now: There is no middle ground: life is found in the Son, and nowhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Water and blood. This is the most debated verse in the chapter. “Water and blood” probably refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death, the public events that mark the beginning and end of his ministry and together declare who he is. At his baptism, the Father declared him Son and the Spirit descended (Mark 1:9–11). At his death, he shed his blood for sins (1:7). Some see a reference to the water and blood that flowed from his side (John 19:34), or to baptism and the Lord’s Supper, but the baptism-and-death reading fits the context best.

In the flow. Verses 6–12 ask how we can be sure that Jesus is the Son of God, and answer with witnesses: the Spirit, the water and the blood (vv. 6–8), which together are God’s own testimony (vv. 9–10) that eternal life is in the Son (vv. 11–12). That leads straight to the purpose of the letter (v. 13).

Not by the water only. The false teachers, like Cerinthus, whom early tradition remembers as John’s opponent in Ephesus, apparently taught that the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism (water) but left before his death (blood), so that only the man Jesus died. John insists that the Son of God himself came through both. The false teaching would happily keep a heavenly Christ who descended on the river bank and spoke beautiful words; it could not bear a Christ who bled. John will not let the blood be taken away, because the blood is where the salvation is.

The Spirit testifies. The Holy Spirit bears witness to Christ: at his baptism, through the apostles’ preaching, through Scripture, and in believers’ hearts (John 15:26; 16:14). The Spirit of truth (John 14:17) bears witness not to a divided Christ but to the one Jesus Christ who is both God and man.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the water of baptism saves. John speaks of Christ’s historical baptism and death as the events that testify to who he is.

Why does it matter that the Son of God himself died, and not only the man Jesus? Because a mere man’s death could pay for, at most, one man’s sins, and not even his own if he were a sinner. The worth of the sacrifice depends on who offers it. Because the one who died was the eternal Son, truly man and truly God in one person, his death has infinite value, enough for all his people of every age (Hebrews 9:14; Acts 20:28). Scripture can even say that they crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). God did not send someone else to suffer while he stayed safe. He came himself.
verseByVerse.note: “Water and blood” probably refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death. John says this against teachers who said the divine Christ left Jesus before the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are three that testify: the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three that testify. “Three”: the Old Testament required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides three, and they agree.

The Spirit and the water and the blood. The Spirit’s testimony is the inward, ongoing witness given to believers (v. 10; 4:13); the water and the blood are the public events at the beginning and end of his ministry.

These three agree. “Agree” (eis to hen eisin) is literally are toward the one thing: all three point the same way. All three bear one witness: Jesus is the Son of God who came in the flesh and died for sins. So where the Son is refused, it is not because God has given too little witness.

Textual note. Some late manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven, known as the Johannine Comma or Comma Johanneum (a comma here means a short clause): “For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth.” They are not found in the text of any Greek manuscript before about the fourteenth century, and then only in a handful. No Greek church father quotes them, even in the fourth-century debates over the Trinity, when they would have been the obvious verse to cite. They appear to have begun as a comment in the margin of some Latin manuscripts that was later copied into the text. Erasmus left them out of the first two editions of his printed Greek New Testament and added them in the third, after a single recent Greek manuscript containing them was produced; from that line of printed texts they passed into the King James Version. However true the statement is in itself, it is almost certainly not part of what John wrote, which is why most modern Bibles omit it or give it only in a footnote. The doctrine of the Trinity does not depend on them; it is taught clearly throughout Scripture (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14; John 1:1; 14:16–17). And the three witnesses John actually gave, Spirit, water and blood, supply all the testimony his argument needs.

Does this mean the Bible has errors, or that I should not use the King James Version? Neither. The Bible as God gave it is without error. God has preserved his word through thousands of manuscripts, more than for any other ancient book, and comparing them lets us see almost exactly what the apostles wrote; the differences between manuscripts are many but mostly tiny (spelling, word order, a small word added or dropped), the few larger ones are well known and marked in modern Bibles, and no doctrine rests on a doubtful reading. Noticing a later addition is part of honouring the original. The King James Version is a noble translation that has fed believers for four centuries, and you can read it with profit, simply knowing that this one sentence was added later. Modern translations mark such places in a footnote.
verseByVerse.note: Some late manuscripts add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven (known from the King James Version). They are not in the early Greek manuscripts and the ESV omits them.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The testimony of men. “Receive” (lambanomen) means accept. We accept human testimony every day: the doctor’s diagnosis, the map, the friend who tells us the road is closed.

The testimony of God is greater. “Greater” (meizōn) means more reliable, more authoritative. God cannot lie (Titus 1:2). If we trust human witnesses, how much more God.

Concerning his Son. “Has borne” (memartyrēken) is perfect tense: has testified and the testimony stands. At the Jordan and on the mountain the Father’s own voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17; 17:5). And in raising him from the dead, God declared him to be the Son of God in power (Romans 1:4).

Where do I hear God’s testimony today? In Scripture, above all. The Father’s voice at the Jordan, the miracles, the empty tomb and the apostles’ witness are all recorded there, and the Bible is God’s own testimony in written form (2 Timothy 3:16). You hear it whenever the word is read and preached. And the Spirit who inspired it confirms it in your heart as you read and hear (v. 10). You do not need a private voice or a vision. Open the Gospels, and God himself is testifying to you about his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The testimony in himself. “Believes in” (pisteuōn eis) is literally trusts into, puts faith in. “Has the testimony in himself”: God’s outward testimony becomes an inward witness in the believer, by the Spirit (Romans 8:16; Galatians 4:6). This is not a private feeling of our own making; it is God’s testimony, confirmed within us.

Made him a liar. Unbelief is not neutral or merely intellectual; it calls God a liar (1:10), a slander against the God who testified. A thoughtful sceptic may protest that he is simply unconvinced. John does not call every question wicked, but he insists that God has not left his Son without witness. When the witness is given and the Son is still refused, the deepest reason is usually not in the head but in the heart, which does not want a Lord: “you refuse to come to me that you may have life,” Jesus said (John 5:40).

Honouring the Son. Unbelief is grave because God’s testimony is about the one he loves most. Jesus said that whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him (John 5:23), and John had written that whoever receives Christ’s testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true (John 3:33). To refuse Jesus is not to decline one religious option among many; it is to tell the Father that his word about his beloved Son is false. To believe in him is the reverse: it is to say amen to God about Jesus.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every doubt is calling God a liar. Honest struggles with doubt are different from settled unbelief (Mark 9:24; Jude 22).

What if I do not sense any inner witness? The inner witness is usually quieter than people expect. It is not normally a voice or a feeling of certainty, but the simple fact that, when you hear the gospel, you find it true and cannot let it go; that Christ is precious to you; that you call God Father; that you want to obey him. That is the Spirit at work (Romans 8:15–16). And the inner witness always rests on the outer one: God’s testimony in Scripture. If your sense of assurance is faint, do not go looking inside yourself for it. Go back to the testimony, read it, and believe it. The inner witness grows as you feed on the outer.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave us eternal life. Here is the content of God’s testimony. “Gave” is past tense: eternal life is a gift already given to believers (John 3:16; 10:28; Romans 6:23).

This life is in his Son. Eternal life is not a thing God hands out apart from Christ; it is found in a person (John 1:4; 14:6), which is why having the Son (v. 12) and having life are the same thing. No formula, ritual, spiritual discipline or religious achievement can transfer the life apart from the Son in whom it lives. The Father could give no greater gift, because he has nothing greater than his Son.

Were Old Testament believers saved through the Son too? Yes. There has only ever been one way of salvation: by grace, through faith, in Christ. Old Testament believers looked forward to the promised Redeemer through the promises and sacrifices God gave, as we look back to him (Romans 4:1–8; Hebrews 11:13, 26; John 8:56). Abraham rejoiced to see Christ’s day; Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures. The life they received was the same life, and it was in the same Son, whose sacrifice covered the sins of his people before his coming as well as after (Romans 3:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has the Son has life. “Has” means possesses, through faith. It is the starkest contrast in the letter: not more or less, but has or does not have.

Does not have life. No Christ, no life. There is no other way (John 3:36; 14:6; Acts 4:12). It is both an open invitation, since anyone from any background may have the Son by faith, and an exclusive claim. To soften it would leave people comfortable while, as John says, they do not have life.

What about someone I loved who died without professing faith? This is one of the hardest questions a Christian carries, and Scripture does not give us a different way of salvation to ease the pain. But it does give you some things to hold. You do not know what happened in that person’s heart, perhaps in the last hours, and God is not bound by what we saw. The Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and he is kinder and wiser than we are. You may grieve and leave them in his hands. And let the grief make you urgent for the living: tell those still with you about the Son, while there is time.

For worship. Life has a name, and the name is Jesus. All the life of God dwells in him, and he gives himself to beggars, to children, to the dying thief, to anyone who comes. There is no one so dead that he cannot make alive, and no one who has him will ever die.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Knowing What We Have in Christ: Assurance, Prayer, and the True God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John states his purpose: that believers may know they have eternal life. Those who know may pray boldly, intercede for a brother who sins, and rest in three closing certainties, ending with Jesus Christ named as the true God. So the last word is a guard against every substitute.
verseByVerse.theology:
That You May Know

Assurance leads to bold prayer, to prayer for others, and to rest in what God has made certain.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The letter closes on Jesus Christ as the true God and eternal life.

Now: Having the true God, refuse every substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things. “These things” are the whole letter. John writes not to evangelise but to assure: his audience already believes, and what they need is confidence in what believing gives them.

That you may know. “Know” (eidēte) means know with settled certainty: not hope, not feel, not reasonably expect, but know. “Have” is present tense: eternal life is a present possession. The tests of the letter are not meant to make believers anxious but to give them assurance: a plain certainty confirmed by the Spirit, unlike the secret knowledge the false teachers claimed. Assurance is not presumption; it is the right response to the reliability of God’s word about his Son.

Two letters, one purpose. The Gospel was written so that you may believe (John 20:31); the letter, so that you who believe may know. The Gospel brings people to the door; the letter tells them they are inside. An old apostle spent his last years making sure that the children of God did not live like orphans. God is not a Father who keeps his sons in suspense about whether they will be thrown out. He has written it down, sealed it with his Son’s blood, and put his Spirit in our hearts to say it to us.

In the name of the Son. Believers can know they have eternal life because it depends not on the strength of their believing but on the one they believe in, and he has spoken plainly about his sheep: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). John had heard those words. The certainty he offers is not confidence in ourselves; it is confidence in Christ’s promise, Christ’s blood and Christ’s grip.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be sure of salvation? Roman Catholic teaching has generally held that, apart from special revelation, no one can be certain of final salvation; some Protestants hold that assurance belongs only to a few mature believers. This commentary’s view: John wrote so that ordinary believers may know they have eternal life. Assurance rests first on God’s promise in Christ (vv. 11–12), is confirmed by the Spirit’s inward witness (v. 10; Romans 8:16), and is supported by the fruit of faith, love and obedience. It is the normal privilege of every Christian, though it may be weak or clouded at times, and it grows as faith grows.

If assurance is normal, why do I lack it? There are several common reasons, and each has a remedy. Some look only at themselves, not at Christ; look first at the promise (vv. 11–12). Some are holding on to a known sin, which clouds the sense of God’s favour; confess it and turn (1:9). Some are going through suffering, depression or exhaustion, which darkens everything; be patient with yourself, and lean on others. Some were taught that doubt is proof of being lost; it is not. The Westminster Confession says that a true believer may wait long and struggle before he has assurance, and may have it shaken, but is never utterly without the seed of faith (Westminster 18.3–4; 1689 18.3–4). Keep coming to Christ. Assurance is the fruit of faith, not its root.
verseByVerse.note: John’s Gospel was written that readers might believe; this letter that believers might know they have eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Confidence toward him. “Confidence” (parrēsia) is boldness, freedom of speech, as in 2:28; 3:21; 4:17. Assurance of eternal life leads at once to boldness in prayer.

According to his will. This is the governing condition of prayer (Matthew 6:10): not bending God to our will but aligning ourselves with his. “Hears” means hears favourably: he who holds the galaxies bends to hear the whisper of a child, and he hears with the intention of giving. We learn his will through Scripture, and the Spirit helps us pray (Romans 8:26–27). The person who knows God through his word can pray with confidence, because he is asking in the direction God is already moving.

Asking in his name. The boldness John describes was given in the upper room. Jesus told his disciples that whatever they asked in his name he would do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son (John 14:13–14). To pray in his name is not to add a formula at the end; it is to come on his merit and ask what he would ask. Our prayers are heard because we come in the name of the Son who is always heard.

Should I add if it be your will to every prayer? Is that a lack of faith? It is not a lack of faith when the matter is one Scripture leaves open, such as healing, a job or a particular outcome; it is humble trust, and Jesus prayed that way in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39). James says we should say, if the Lord wills (James 4:15). But where God has plainly revealed his will, there is no need to hedge: pray boldly that he will forgive, make you holy, give you wisdom (James 1:5), spread the gospel, and keep his people. The phrase should never be a way of expecting nothing. It is the trust of a child who asks freely and lets his Father decide.

verseByVerse.quote: And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He hears us. For John, to be heard by God is to be answered.

We have the requests. “Have” (echomen) is present tense: the answer is as good as given, even before we see it. If a prayer is according to his will, God hears it and grants it, in his time and way (Mark 11:24). This is not a blank cheque for anything we care to ask; it is the confidence of a person whose asking has been shaped by the God he knows.

Every promise is Yes in him. The answer is anchored in Christ, not in the strength of the asking. All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20), and he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all will graciously give us all things with him (Romans 8:32). The cross is the pledge behind every answered prayer.

Daniel’s three weeks. Daniel mourned, prayed and fasted for three weeks, and when the answer finally came, the messenger told him: from the first day that you set your heart to understand, your words have been heard, and I have come because of your words (Daniel 10:12). Delay is not refusal, and silence is not deafness.

If God has already heard, why keep praying about the same thing? Because Jesus told us to. He told the parable of the widow who kept coming to the judge, to show that we ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1–8), and he taught us to ask, seek and knock, all continuous (Matthew 7:7). Persistent prayer is not nagging an unwilling God but trusting a willing one, and it changes us as we wait: it deepens our desire, purifies our motives, and keeps us dependent on him. Keep praying until God answers or shows you that his answer is different from what you asked.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sin not leading to death. This is the most contested passage in the letter. The confident intercession of verses 14–15 is applied at once to a sinning brother in the church. “Not leading to death” (mē pros thanaton) is sin that does not end in spiritual death: most likely the ordinary failures and sins of genuine believers, for which repentance and forgiveness remain available (1:9).

God will give him life. God answers intercession by restoring and sustaining the sinning believer’s spiritual life. God gives life through the prayers of his people.

Sin that leads to death. The sin that leads to death is probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by the false teachers who left the church (2:19, 22): a deliberate, persistent denial of the Son despite knowing the truth, akin to the blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:29) and the apostasy of Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26. John does not forbid praying for such people; he simply does not command it.

All wrongdoing is sin. John makes light of no sin. But the sins of believers who remain in Christ do not lead to spiritual death, because his blood cleanses them (1:7).

I have prayed for you. The church’s prayer for a stumbling brother copies something Christ does. On the night Peter would deny him, Jesus said, Simon, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:31–32). Peter fell, but his faith did not die. When believers pray for a sinning brother and God gives life, they are praying in step with Christ, our Advocate with the Father (2:1), who always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

Where Christians differ: what is the sin that leads to death? Roman Catholic teaching distinguishes mortal sins (which destroy grace and lead to death unless confessed) from venial sins. Others think John means a sin punished by physical death under God’s hand of discipline (Acts 5:1–11, Ananias and Sapphira; 1 Corinthians 11:30), or the unpardonable sin of blaspheming the Spirit (Matthew 12:31–32); and the honest truth is that we cannot be dogmatic about every detail. This commentary’s view: In context, the sin leading to death is not a category of especially bad acts that a believer may commit and so lose salvation, but the settled apostasy of those who deny Jesus is the Christ, as the false teachers did. True believers, born of God, are kept from it (v. 18). There is no list of mortal sins that sends a genuine believer to hell; all their sins are covered by Christ’s propitiation (2:1–2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can know with certainty that someone has committed the sin that leads to death, so that we should give up on them. That judgment belongs to God.

Could I have committed the sin that leads to death? If you are worried that you have, that worry is strong evidence that you have not. The sin John means is a settled, hardened rejection of Christ by people who no longer care, who have walked away and want nothing more to do with him. A person who fears he has sinned beyond forgiveness and still wants Christ is not that person. The very desire to be forgiven is the work of the Spirit, who does not work in the hearts of the finally hardened. Come to Christ now. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37), and that promise has no exception clause.

In everyday life. If a fellow believer is struggling with sin, pray for him by name instead of talking about him. And if the Lord gives you the opportunity, go to him gently, as one who could fall the same way (Galatians 6:1).
verseByVerse.note: The “sin that leads to death” is probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by those who left the church.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know. This is the first of three closing certainties (vv. 18, 19, 20), three hammer blows of assurance.

Does not keep on sinning. As in 3:6, 9: the present tense means habitual, settled sin.

He protects him. “He who was born of God” (ho gennētheis ek tou theou) is Christ, the eternal Son of the Father. Some manuscripts read “protects himself”, meaning the believer, but the better reading points to Christ. The believer does not keep himself safe; Christ keeps him (John 10:28; Jude 24), as he said on the last night: “While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost” (John 17:12). The hand that holds us bears the marks of the nails.

The evil one does not touch him. “Touch” (haptetai) means seize so as to harm. Satan may tempt and attack, but he cannot drag the believer back into his power. This is what is called the perseverance of the saints: Christ keeps every true believer to the end. The believer is not spared attack, but he cannot finally be defeated.

Does this mean Satan cannot harm me at all, through illness or persecution? Not quite. Job was afflicted in body, family and possessions with God’s permission, and Paul received a messenger of Satan to harass him (2 Corinthians 12:7). Believers are tested, persecuted and sometimes killed (Revelation 2:10). But Satan works only within the limits God sets, and he cannot touch the life that is in Christ. He could take Job’s health but not his God; he could kill the martyrs but not separate them from Christ’s love (Romans 8:38–39). The worst he can do to the body becomes, in God’s hands, the means of bringing his child home.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that we are from God. The second certainty. “From God” (ek tou theou) means born of him, belonging to him.

The whole world lies. “Lies” (keitai) pictures passive lying, like someone asleep in another’s arms. “In the power of the evil one” (en tō ponērō) is literally in the evil one. The world is under Satan’s influence (2 Corinthians 4:4; Ephesians 2:2), not fighting him but resting in his embrace, unaware.

Lifted up to draw. The verse that names the world’s captor goes straight on to name its rescuer. “Now will the ruler of this world be cast out,” Jesus said. “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:31–32). The world lies passive in the evil one’s grip and cannot climb out. But the Son lifted up on the cross is drawing people out of every nation, and those who are from God are the ones he has drawn. To be from God is to have been pulled out by a crucified hand.

How should I treat a world that lies in the evil one? Should I withdraw? No. Jesus prayed not that the Father would take us out of the world, but that he would keep us from the evil one (John 17:15), and he sent us into it (John 17:18). The world is not to be feared, despised or imitated, but loved and reached. Your unbelieving neighbours are not the enemy; they are captives of the enemy, asleep in his arms, and the gospel is the voice that wakes them. So be in the world as a light, not a mirror: work well, love well, speak of Christ, and refuse its idols. Separation from sin, yes; separation from sinners, no.

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we know that the Son of God has come. The third certainty, and the greatest. “Has come” (hēkei) means has arrived and is present. The incarnation with which the letter opened (1:1–2) is the ground of everything.

Understanding. “Understanding” (dianoian) is mind, insight, the capacity to grasp. Not secret knowledge for an elite but a renewed mind given to all believers.

Him who is true. “Him who is true” (ton alēthinon) is the genuine one, the real one: God the Father, in contrast with false gods (John 17:3).

In his Son. We are in the Father by being in his Son; no one is joined to the one without the other.

The true God and eternal life. “He” (houtos, this one) most naturally refers to Jesus Christ, the person named just before. It is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s deity in the New Testament, alongside John 1:1 and 20:28, and it brings the letter back to where it began: the eternal life that was made manifest (1:2) is the true God himself.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus called the true God here? Some, including Jehovah’s Witnesses and some scholars, take he to refer to the Father. This commentary’s view: Grammatically, this one most naturally refers to the nearest person, Jesus Christ. John has just called Jesus eternal life (1:2), and his Gospel calls Jesus God (John 1:1, 18; 20:28). The letter that opens with the eternal life made visible closes by naming him the true God. Jesus is fully God, one with the Father, as the church confesses.

Thomas’s confession. John’s Gospel reaches its height when Thomas, faced with the risen Jesus and his wounds, says, my Lord and my God! (John 20:28). Jesus did not correct him, and the letter reaches its height in the same place. The apostle who leaned on his chest at supper ends his letter on his knees.

How can Jesus be the true God when he prayed to the Father? Because God is one being in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet one God (Matthew 28:19). The Son praying to the Father is not one God praying to another, nor God praying to himself, but one divine person speaking to another within the one life of God. And as man, the Son truly prayed, depended and obeyed, as our representative. The incarnation did not make him less God; it made him also man. Scripture holds both together: I and the Father are one (John 10:30), and the Father is greater than I (John 14:28), the second spoken of his humble state as man.

For worship. He is the true God. The baby who was laid in a manger, the man who wept and slept and bled, is the living and true God, Creator of all, before whom angels veil their faces. And he is eternal life, not merely its giver but its very self. We are in him, held by the one who made the stars and bore our sins, and there is nothing truer to worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep yourselves from idols. It is one of the most abrupt closings in the New Testament, and exactly right: after declaring Jesus the true God (v. 20), John warns against every false god. In Ephesus, where John probably wrote, the temple of Artemis and emperor worship meant literal idols were everywhere. The word also covers the false Christ of the false teachers, a god made in their own image, and anything we put in God’s place: money, pleasure, status, self (Colossians 3:5). Christ keeps us (v. 18), and we are to keep ourselves. The best protection is the deep knowledge of the one who is true. You cannot treasure the real and be satisfied with the counterfeit. Every idol promises what only he can give and gives nothing back but emptiness.

The last word of an old man. Fathers who know they are dying say the thing that matters most. John ends not with a blessing but with a warning, spoken with the tenderest name he has: little children. He knew how easily the heart drifts to substitutes. Calvin said the human mind is a perpetual forge of idols, a workshop that never stops making them. The old apostle’s final act of love was to stand at its door and warn us.

How do I recognise an idol in my own life? An idol is anything you look to for what only God can give: security, identity, meaning, comfort, approval. Ask some searching questions. What do I worry about losing most? What do I daydream about? Where does my money go first? What makes me angry when it is threatened? What do I turn to when I am anxious or sad? Whose approval do I most crave? An idol is usually a good thing made into a god thing: a child, a career, a body, a reputation, a cause. The answer is not merely to smash the idol but to love Christ more, so that it shrinks back to its proper size.

5.theology:
Faith as Victory. In 5:4 the victory that overcomes the world is “our faith.” Faith is not a spiritual achievement but a hand that receives, a trust that looks away from itself to the Son of God who has already overcome.

Assurance as Gift. John writes “that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). Assurance is not presumption. Presumption claims safety without grounds; assurance rests on the promises of God, the witness of the Spirit and the evidence of new birth.
5.examples:
Then: A church battered by false teaching and painful departures needed to know that the life they had received in the Son was real and eternal. John gave them not a new experience but the settled confidence of those who have the Son.

Now: Assurance in John is not a feeling to be worked up but a knowledge to be received, grounded in God’s testimony about his Son (5:9–10). Whoever has the Son has life, and the Son cannot be taken away.
